/repo/guides/source/action_mailer_basics.md file 1: **DO NOT READ THIS FILE ON GITHUB, GUIDES ARE PUBLISHED ON https://guides.rubyonrails.org.** 2: 3: Action Mailer Basics 4: ==================== 5: 6: This guide provides you with all you need to get started in sending 7: emails from your application, and many internals of Action 8: Mailer. It also covers how to test your mailers. 9: 10: After reading this guide, you will know: 11: 12: * How to send email within a Rails application. 13: * How to generate and edit an Action Mailer class and mailer view. 14: * How to configure Action Mailer for your environment. 15: * How to test your Action Mailer classes. 16: 17: -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 18: 19: What is Action Mailer? 20: ---------------------- 21: 22: Action Mailer allows you to send emails from your application using mailer classes 23: and views. 24: 25: ### Mailers are Similar to Controllers 26: 27: They inherit from [`ActionMailer::Base`][] and live in `app/mailers`. Mailers also work 28: very similarly to controllers. Some examples of similarities are enumerated below. 29: Mailers have: 30: 31: * Actions, and also, associated views that appear in `app/views`. 32: * Instance variables that are accessible in views. 33: * The ability to utilise layouts and partials. 34: * The ability to access a params hash. 35: 36: [`ActionMailer::Base`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html 37: 38: Sending Emails 39: -------------- 40: 41: This section will provide a step-by-step guide to creating a mailer and its 42: views. 43: 44: ### Walkthrough to Generating a Mailer 45: 46: #### Create the Mailer 47: 48: ```bash 49: $ bin/rails generate mailer User 50: create app/mailers/user_mailer.rb 51: create app/mailers/application_mailer.rb 52: invoke erb 53: create app/views/user_mailer 54: create app/views/layouts/mailer.text.erb 55: create app/views/layouts/mailer.html.erb 56: invoke test_unit 57: create test/mailers/user_mailer_test.rb 58: create test/mailers/previews/user_mailer_preview.rb 59: ``` 60: 61: ```ruby 62: # app/mailers/application_mailer.rb 63: class ApplicationMailer < ActionMailer::Base 64: default from: "from@example.com" 65: layout 'mailer' 66: end 67: ``` 68: 69: ```ruby 70: # app/mailers/user_mailer.rb 71: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 72: end 73: ``` 74: 75: As you can see, you can generate mailers just like you use other generators with 76: Rails. 77: 78: If you didn't want to use a generator, you could create your own file inside of 79: `app/mailers`, just make sure that it inherits from `ActionMailer::Base`: 80: 81: ```ruby 82: class MyMailer < ActionMailer::Base 83: end 84: ``` 85: 86: #### Edit the Mailer 87: 88: Mailers have methods called "actions" and they use views to structure their content. 89: Where a controller generates content like HTML to send back to the client, a Mailer 90: creates a message to be delivered via email. 91: 92: `app/mailers/user_mailer.rb` contains an empty mailer: 93: 94: ```ruby 95: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 96: end 97: ``` 98: 99: Let's add a method called `welcome_email`, that will send an email to the user's 100: registered email address: 101: 102: ```ruby 103: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 104: default from: 'notifications@example.com' 105: 106: def welcome_email 107: @user = params[:user] 108: @url = 'http://example.com/login' 109: mail(to: @user.email, subject: 'Welcome to My Awesome Site') 110: end 111: end 112: ``` 113: 114: Here is a quick explanation of the items presented in the preceding method. For 115: a full list of all available options, please have a look further down at the 116: Complete List of Action Mailer user-settable attributes section. 117: 118: * The [`default`][] method sets default values for all emails sent from 119: this mailer. In this case, we use it to set the `:from` header value for all 120: messages in this class. This can be overridden on a per-email basis. 121: * The [`mail`][] method creates the actual email message. We use it to specify 122: the values of headers like `:to` and `:subject` per email. 123: 124: [`default`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-c-default 125: [`mail`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-mail 126: 127: #### Create a Mailer View 128: 129: Create a file called `welcome_email.html.erb` in `app/views/user_mailer/`. This 130: will be the template used for the email, formatted in HTML: 131: 132: ```html+erb 133: 134: 135: 136: 137: 138: 139:

Welcome to example.com, <%= @user.name %>

140:

141: You have successfully signed up to example.com, 142: your username is: <%= @user.login %>.
143:

144:

145: To login to the site, just follow this link: <%= @url %>. 146:

147:

Thanks for joining and have a great day!

148: 149: 150: ``` 151: 152: Let's also make a text part for this email. Not all clients prefer HTML emails, 153: and so sending both is best practice. To do this, create a file called 154: `welcome_email.text.erb` in `app/views/user_mailer/`: 155: 156: ```erb 157: Welcome to example.com, <%= @user.name %> 158: =============================================== 159: 160: You have successfully signed up to example.com, 161: your username is: <%= @user.login %>. 162: 163: To login to the site, just follow this link: <%= @url %>. 164: 165: Thanks for joining and have a great day! 166: ``` 167: 168: When you call the `mail` method now, Action Mailer will detect the two templates 169: (text and HTML) and automatically generate a `multipart/alternative` email. 170: 171: #### Calling the Mailer 172: 173: Mailers are really just another way to render a view. Instead of rendering a 174: view and sending it over the HTTP protocol, they are sending it out through 175: the email protocols instead. Due to this, it makes sense to have your 176: controller tell the Mailer to send an email when a user is successfully created. 177: 178: Setting this up is simple. 179: 180: First, let's create a `User` scaffold: 181: 182: ```bash 183: $ bin/rails generate scaffold user name email login 184: $ bin/rails db:migrate 185: ``` 186: 187: Now that we have a user model to play with, we will edit the 188: `app/controllers/users_controller.rb` file, make it instruct the `UserMailer` to deliver 189: an email to the newly created user by editing the create action and inserting a 190: call to `UserMailer.with(user: @user).welcome_email` right after the user is successfully saved. 191: 192: We will enqueue the email to be sent by using [`deliver_later`][], which is 193: backed by Active Job. That way, the controller action can continue without 194: waiting for the send to complete. 195: 196: ```ruby 197: class UsersController < ApplicationController 198: # ... 199: 200: # POST /users or /users.json 201: def create 202: @user = User.new(user_params) 203: 204: respond_to do |format| 205: if @user.save 206: # Tell the UserMailer to send a welcome email after save 207: UserMailer.with(user: @user).welcome_email.deliver_later 208: 209: format.html { redirect_to(@user, notice: 'User was successfully created.') } 210: format.json { render json: @user, status: :created, location: @user } 211: else 212: format.html { render action: 'new' } 213: format.json { render json: @user.errors, status: :unprocessable_entity } 214: end 215: end 216: end 217: 218: # ... 219: end 220: ``` 221: 222: NOTE: Active Job's default behavior is to execute jobs via the `:async` adapter. 223: So, you can use `deliver_later` to send emails asynchronously. 224: Active Job's default adapter runs jobs with an in-process thread pool. 225: It's well-suited for the development/test environments, since it doesn't require 226: any external infrastructure, but it's a poor fit for production since it drops 227: pending jobs on restart. 228: If you need a persistent backend, you will need to use an Active Job adapter 229: that has a persistent backend (Sidekiq, Resque, etc). 230: 231: If you want to send emails right away (from a cronjob for example) just call 232: [`deliver_now`][]: 233: 234: ```ruby 235: class SendWeeklySummary 236: def run 237: User.find_each do |user| 238: UserMailer.with(user: user).weekly_summary.deliver_now 239: end 240: end 241: end 242: ``` 243: 244: Any key-value pair passed to [`with`][] just becomes the `params` for the mailer 245: action. So `with(user: @user, account: @user.account)` makes `params[:user]` and 246: `params[:account]` available in the mailer action. Just like controllers have 247: params. 248: 249: The method `weekly_summary` returns an [`ActionMailer::MessageDelivery`][] object which 250: can then be told to `deliver_now` or `deliver_later` to send itself out. The 251: `ActionMailer::MessageDelivery` object is a wrapper around a [`Mail::Message`][]. If 252: you want to inspect, alter, or do anything else with the `Mail::Message` object you can 253: access it with the [`message`][] method on the `ActionMailer::MessageDelivery` object. 254: 255: [`ActionMailer::MessageDelivery`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html 256: [`deliver_later`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html#method-i-deliver_later 257: [`deliver_now`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html#method-i-deliver_now 258: [`Mail::Message`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Mail/Message.html 259: [`message`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html#method-i-message 260: [`with`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Parameterized/ClassMethods.html#method-i-with 261: 262: ### Auto Encoding Header Values 263: 264: Action Mailer handles the auto encoding of multibyte characters inside of 265: headers and bodies. 266: 267: For more complex examples such as defining alternate character sets or 268: self-encoding text first, please refer to the 269: [Mail](https://github.com/mikel/mail) library. 270: 271: ### Complete List of Action Mailer Methods 272: 273: There are just three methods that you need to send pretty much any email 274: message: 275: 276: * [`headers`][] - Specifies any header on the email you want. You can pass a hash of 277: header field names and value pairs, or you can call `headers[:field_name] = 278: 'value'`. 279: * [`attachments`][] - Allows you to add attachments to your email. For example, 280: `attachments['file-name.jpg'] = File.read('file-name.jpg')`. 281: * [`mail`][] - Creates the actual email itself. You can pass in headers as a hash to 282: the `mail` method as a parameter. `mail` will create an email — either plain 283: text or multipart — depending on what email templates you have defined. 284: 285: [`attachments`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-attachments 286: [`headers`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-headers 287: 288: #### Adding Attachments 289: 290: Action Mailer makes it very easy to add attachments. 291: 292: * Pass the file name and content and Action Mailer and the 293: [Mail gem](https://github.com/mikel/mail) will automatically guess the 294: `mime_type`, set the `encoding`, and create the attachment. 295: 296: ```ruby 297: attachments['filename.jpg'] = File.read('/path/to/filename.jpg') 298: ``` 299: 300: When the `mail` method will be triggered, it will send a multipart email with 301: an attachment, properly nested with the top level being `multipart/mixed` and 302: the first part being a `multipart/alternative` containing the plain text and 303: HTML email messages. 304: 305: NOTE: Mail will automatically Base64 encode an attachment. If you want something 306: different, encode your content and pass in the encoded content and encoding in a 307: `Hash` to the `attachments` method. 308: 309: * Pass the file name and specify headers and content and Action Mailer and Mail 310: will use the settings you pass in. 311: 312: ```ruby 313: encoded_content = SpecialEncode(File.read('/path/to/filename.jpg')) 314: attachments['filename.jpg'] = { 315: mime_type: 'application/gzip', 316: encoding: 'SpecialEncoding', 317: content: encoded_content 318: } 319: ``` 320: 321: NOTE: If you specify an encoding, Mail will assume that your content is already 322: encoded and not try to Base64 encode it. 323: 324: #### Making Inline Attachments 325: 326: Action Mailer 3.0 makes inline attachments, which involved a lot of hacking in pre 3.0 versions, much simpler and trivial as they should be. 327: 328: * First, to tell Mail to turn an attachment into an inline attachment, you just call `#inline` on the attachments method within your Mailer: 329: 330: ```ruby 331: def welcome 332: attachments.inline['image.jpg'] = File.read('/path/to/image.jpg') 333: end 334: ``` 335: 336: * Then in your view, you can just reference `attachments` as a hash and specify 337: which attachment you want to show, calling `url` on it and then passing the 338: result into the `image_tag` method: 339: 340: ```html+erb 341:

Hello there, this is our image

342: 343: <%= image_tag attachments['image.jpg'].url %> 344: ``` 345: 346: * As this is a standard call to `image_tag` you can pass in an options hash 347: after the attachment URL as you could for any other image: 348: 349: ```html+erb 350:

Hello there, this is our image

351: 352: <%= image_tag attachments['image.jpg'].url, alt: 'My Photo', class: 'photos' %> 353: ``` 354: 355: #### Sending Email to Multiple Recipients 356: 357: It is possible to send email to one or more recipients in one email (e.g., 358: informing all admins of a new signup) by setting the list of emails to the `:to` 359: key. The list of emails can be an array of email addresses or a single string 360: with the addresses separated by commas. 361: 362: ```ruby 363: class AdminMailer < ApplicationMailer 364: default to: -> { Admin.pluck(:email) }, 365: from: 'notification@example.com' 366: 367: def new_registration(user) 368: @user = user 369: mail(subject: "New User Signup: #{@user.email}") 370: end 371: end 372: ``` 373: 374: The same format can be used to set carbon copy (Cc:) and blind carbon copy 375: (Bcc:) recipients, by using the `:cc` and `:bcc` keys respectively. 376: 377: #### Sending Email with Name 378: 379: Sometimes you wish to show the name of the person instead of just their email 380: address when they receive the email. You can use [`email_address_with_name`][] for 381: that: 382: 383: ```ruby 384: def welcome_email 385: @user = params[:user] 386: mail( 387: to: email_address_with_name(@user.email, @user.name), 388: subject: 'Welcome to My Awesome Site' 389: ) 390: end 391: ``` 392: 393: The same technique works to specify a sender name: 394: 395: ```ruby 396: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 397: default from: email_address_with_name('notification@example.com', 'Example Company Notifications') 398: end 399: ``` 400: 401: If the name is a blank string, it returns just the address. 402: 403: [`email_address_with_name`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-email_address_with_name 404: 405: ### Mailer Views 406: 407: Mailer views are located in the `app/views/name_of_mailer_class` directory. The 408: specific mailer view is known to the class because its name is the same as the 409: mailer method. In our example from above, our mailer view for the 410: `welcome_email` method will be in `app/views/user_mailer/welcome_email.html.erb` 411: for the HTML version and `welcome_email.text.erb` for the plain text version. 412: 413: To change the default mailer view for your action you do something like: 414: 415: ```ruby 416: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 417: default from: 'notifications@example.com' 418: 419: def welcome_email 420: @user = params[:user] 421: @url = 'http://example.com/login' 422: mail(to: @user.email, 423: subject: 'Welcome to My Awesome Site', 424: template_path: 'notifications', 425: template_name: 'another') 426: end 427: end 428: ``` 429: 430: In this case, it will look for templates at `app/views/notifications` with name 431: `another`. You can also specify an array of paths for `template_path`, and they 432: will be searched in order. 433: 434: If you want more flexibility you can also pass a block and render specific 435: templates or even render inline or text without using a template file: 436: 437: ```ruby 438: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 439: default from: 'notifications@example.com' 440: 441: def welcome_email 442: @user = params[:user] 443: @url = 'http://example.com/login' 444: mail(to: @user.email, 445: subject: 'Welcome to My Awesome Site') do |format| 446: format.html { render 'another_template' } 447: format.text { render plain: 'Render text' } 448: end 449: end 450: end 451: ``` 452: 453: This will render the template 'another_template.html.erb' for the HTML part and 454: use the rendered text for the text part. The render command is the same one used 455: inside of Action Controller, so you can use all the same options, such as 456: `:text`, `:inline`, etc. 457: 458: If you would like to render a template located outside of the default `app/views/mailer_name/` directory, you can apply the [`prepend_view_path`][], like so: 459: 460: ```ruby 461: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 462: prepend_view_path "custom/path/to/mailer/view" 463: 464: # This will try to load "custom/path/to/mailer/view/welcome_email" template 465: def welcome_email 466: # ... 467: end 468: end 469: ``` 470: 471: You can also consider using the [`append_view_path`][] method. 472: 473: [`append_view_path`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/ViewPaths/ClassMethods.html#method-i-append_view_path 474: [`prepend_view_path`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/ViewPaths/ClassMethods.html#method-i-prepend_view_path 475: 476: #### Caching Mailer View 477: 478: You can perform fragment caching in mailer views like in application views using the [`cache`][] method. 479: 480: ```html+erb 481: <% cache do %> 482: <%= @company.name %> 483: <% end %> 484: ``` 485: 486: And to use this feature, you need to configure your application with this: 487: 488: ```ruby 489: config.action_mailer.perform_caching = true 490: ``` 491: 492: Fragment caching is also supported in multipart emails. 493: Read more about caching in the [Rails caching guide](caching_with_rails.html). 494: 495: [`cache`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/Helpers/CacheHelper.html#method-i-cache 496: 497: ### Action Mailer Layouts 498: 499: Just like controller views, you can also have mailer layouts. The layout name 500: needs to be the same as your mailer, such as `user_mailer.html.erb` and 501: `user_mailer.text.erb` to be automatically recognized by your mailer as a 502: layout. 503: 504: To use a different file, call [`layout`][] in your mailer: 505: 506: ```ruby 507: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 508: layout 'awesome' # use awesome.(html|text).erb as the layout 509: end 510: ``` 511: 512: Just like with controller views, use `yield` to render the view inside the 513: layout. 514: 515: You can also pass in a `layout: 'layout_name'` option to the render call inside 516: the format block to specify different layouts for different formats: 517: 518: ```ruby 519: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 520: def welcome_email 521: mail(to: params[:user].email) do |format| 522: format.html { render layout: 'my_layout' } 523: format.text 524: end 525: end 526: end 527: ``` 528: 529: Will render the HTML part using the `my_layout.html.erb` file and the text part 530: with the usual `user_mailer.text.erb` file if it exists. 531: 532: [`layout`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/Layouts/ClassMethods.html#method-i-layout 533: 534: ### Previewing Emails 535: 536: Action Mailer previews provide a way to see how emails look by visiting a 537: special URL that renders them. In the above example, the preview class for 538: `UserMailer` should be named `UserMailerPreview` and located in 539: `test/mailers/previews/user_mailer_preview.rb`. To see the preview of 540: `welcome_email`, implement a method that has the same name and call 541: `UserMailer.welcome_email`: 542: 543: ```ruby 544: class UserMailerPreview < ActionMailer::Preview 545: def welcome_email 546: UserMailer.with(user: User.first).welcome_email 547: end 548: end 549: ``` 550: 551: Then the preview will be available in . 552: 553: If you change something in `app/views/user_mailer/welcome_email.html.erb` 554: or the mailer itself, it'll automatically reload and render it so you can 555: visually see the new style instantly. A list of previews are also available 556: in . 557: 558: By default, these preview classes live in `test/mailers/previews`. 559: This can be configured using the `preview_paths` option. For example, if you 560: want to add `lib/mailer_previews` to it, you can configure it in 561: `config/application.rb`: 562: 563: ```ruby 564: config.action_mailer.preview_paths << "#{Rails.root}/lib/mailer_previews" 565: ``` 566: 567: ### Generating URLs in Action Mailer Views 568: 569: Unlike controllers, the mailer instance doesn't have any context about the 570: incoming request so you'll need to provide the `:host` parameter yourself. 571: 572: As the `:host` usually is consistent across the application you can configure it 573: globally in `config/application.rb`: 574: 575: ```ruby 576: config.action_mailer.default_url_options = { host: 'example.com' } 577: ``` 578: 579: Because of this behavior, you cannot use any of the `*_path` helpers inside of 580: an email. Instead, you will need to use the associated `*_url` helper. For example 581: instead of using 582: 583: ```html+erb 584: <%= link_to 'welcome', welcome_path %> 585: ``` 586: 587: You will need to use: 588: 589: ```html+erb 590: <%= link_to 'welcome', welcome_url %> 591: ``` 592: 593: By using the full URL, your links will now work in your emails. 594: 595: #### Generating URLs with `url_for` 596: 597: [`url_for`][] generates a full URL by default in templates. 598: 599: If you did not configure the `:host` option globally make sure to pass it to 600: `url_for`. 601: 602: 603: ```erb 604: <%= url_for(host: 'example.com', 605: controller: 'welcome', 606: action: 'greeting') %> 607: ``` 608: 609: [`url_for`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/RoutingUrlFor.html#method-i-url_for 610: 611: #### Generating URLs with Named Routes 612: 613: Email clients have no web context and so paths have no base URL to form complete 614: web addresses. Thus, you should always use the `*_url` variant of named route 615: helpers. 616: 617: If you did not configure the `:host` option globally make sure to pass it to the 618: URL helper. 619: 620: ```erb 621: <%= user_url(@user, host: 'example.com') %> 622: ``` 623: 624: ### Adding Images in Action Mailer Views 625: 626: Unlike controllers, the mailer instance doesn't have any context about the 627: incoming request so you'll need to provide the `:asset_host` parameter yourself. 628: 629: As the `:asset_host` usually is consistent across the application you can 630: configure it globally in `config/application.rb`: 631: 632: ```ruby 633: config.action_mailer.asset_host = 'http://example.com' 634: ``` 635: 636: NOTE: Because we can't infer the protocol from the request, you'll need to 637: specify a protocol such as `http://` or `https://` in the 638: `:asset_host` config. 639: 640: Now you can display an image inside your email. 641: 642: ```html+erb 643: <%= image_tag 'image.jpg' %> 644: ``` 645: 646: ### Sending Multipart Emails 647: 648: Action Mailer will automatically send multipart emails if you have different 649: templates for the same action. So, for our `UserMailer` example, if you have 650: `welcome_email.text.erb` and `welcome_email.html.erb` in 651: `app/views/user_mailer`, Action Mailer will automatically send a multipart email 652: with the HTML and text versions setup as different parts. 653: 654: The order of the parts getting inserted is determined by the `:parts_order` 655: inside of the `ActionMailer::Base.default` method. 656: 657: ### Sending Emails with Dynamic Delivery Options 658: 659: If you wish to override the default delivery options (e.g. SMTP credentials) 660: while delivering emails, you can do this using `delivery_method_options` in the 661: mailer action. 662: 663: ```ruby 664: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 665: def welcome_email 666: @user = params[:user] 667: @url = user_url(@user) 668: delivery_options = { user_name: params[:company].smtp_user, 669: password: params[:company].smtp_password, 670: address: params[:company].smtp_host } 671: mail(to: @user.email, 672: subject: "Please see the Terms and Conditions attached", 673: delivery_method_options: delivery_options) 674: end 675: end 676: ``` 677: 678: ### Sending Emails without Template Rendering 679: 680: There may be cases in which you want to skip the template rendering step and 681: supply the email body as a string. You can achieve this using the `:body` 682: option. In such cases don't forget to add the `:content_type` option. Rails 683: will default to `text/plain` otherwise. 684: 685: ```ruby 686: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer 687: def welcome_email 688: mail(to: params[:user].email, 689: body: params[:email_body], 690: content_type: "text/html", 691: subject: "Already rendered!") 692: end 693: end 694: ``` 695: 696: Action Mailer Callbacks 697: ----------------------- 698: 699: Action Mailer allows for you to specify a [`before_action`][], [`after_action`][] and 700: [`around_action`][] to configure the message, and [`before_deliver`][], [`after_deliver`][] and 701: [`around_deliver`][] to control the delivery. 702: 703: * Callbacks can be specified with a block or a symbol to a method in the mailer 704: class similar to controllers. 705: 706: * You could use a `before_action` to set instance variables, populate the mail 707: object with defaults, or insert default headers and attachments. 708: 709: ```ruby 710: class InvitationsMailer < ApplicationMailer 711: before_action :set_inviter_and_invitee 712: before_action { @account = params[:inviter].account } 713: 714: default to: -> { @invitee.email_address }, 715: from: -> { common_address(@inviter) }, 716: reply_to: -> { @inviter.email_address_with_name } 717: 718: def account_invitation 719: mail subject: "#{@inviter.name} invited you to their Basecamp (#{@account.name})" 720: end 721: 722: def project_invitation 723: @project = params[:project] 724: @summarizer = ProjectInvitationSummarizer.new(@project.bucket) 725: 726: mail subject: "#{@inviter.name.familiar} added you to a project in Basecamp (#{@account.name})" 727: end 728: 729: private 730: def set_inviter_and_invitee 731: @inviter = params[:inviter] 732: @invitee = params[:invitee] 733: end 734: end 735: ``` 736: 737: * You could use 41:   #     end
42:   #   end

1955: Testing Your Mailers
1956: --------------------
1957: 
1958: Testing mailer classes requires some specific tools to do a thorough job.
1959: 
1960: ### Keeping the Postman in Check
1961: 
1962: Your mailer classes - like every other part of your Rails application - should be tested to ensure that they are working as expected.
1963: 
1964: The goals of testing your mailer classes are to ensure that:
1965: 
1966: * emails are being processed (created and sent)
1967: * the email content is correct (subject, sender, body, etc)
1968: * the right emails are being sent at the right times
1969: 
1970: #### From All Sides
1971: 
1972: There are two aspects of testing your mailer, the unit tests and the functional tests. In the unit tests, you run the mailer in isolation with tightly controlled inputs and compare the output to a known value (a fixture). In the functional tests you don't so much test the minute details produced by the mailer; instead, we test that our controllers and models are using the mailer in the right way. You test to prove that the right email was sent at the right time.
1973: 
1974: ### Unit Testing
1975: 
1976: In order to test that your mailer is working as expected, you can use unit tests to compare the actual results of the mailer with pre-written examples of what should be produced.
1977: 
1978: #### Revenge of the Fixtures
1979: 
1980: For the purposes of unit testing a mailer, fixtures are used to provide an example of how the output _should_ look. Because these are example emails, and not Active Record data like the other fixtures, they are kept in their own subdirectory apart from the other fixtures. The name of the directory within `test/fixtures` directly corresponds to the name of the mailer. So, for a mailer named `UserMailer`, the fixtures should reside in `test/fixtures/user_mailer` directory.
1981: 
1982: If you generated your mailer, the generator does not create stub fixtures for the mailers actions. You'll have to create those files yourself as described above.
1983: 
1984: #### The Basic Test Case
1985: 
1986: Here's a unit test to test a mailer named `UserMailer` whose action `invite` is used to send an invitation to a friend. It is an adapted version of the base test created by the generator for an `invite` action.
1987: 
1988: ```ruby
1989: require "test_helper"
1990: 
1991: class UserMailerTest < ActionMailer::TestCase
1992:   test "invite" do
1993:     # Create the email and store it for further assertions
1994:     email = UserMailer.create_invite("me@example.com",
1995:                                      "friend@example.com", Time.now)
1996: 
1997:     # Send the email, then test that it got queued
1998:     assert_emails 1 do
1999:       email.deliver_now
2000:     end
2001: 
2002:     # Test the body of the sent email contains what we expect it to
2003:     assert_equal ["me@example.com"], email.from
2004:     assert_equal ["friend@example.com"], email.to
2005:     assert_equal "You have been invited by me@example.com", email.subject
2006:     assert_equal read_fixture("invite").join, email.body.to_s
2007:   end
2008: end
2009: ```
2010: 
2011: In the test we create the email and store the returned object in the `email` variable. We then ensure that it was sent (the first assert), then, in the second batch of assertions, we ensure that the email does indeed contain what we expect. The helper `read_fixture` is used to read in the content from this file.
2012: 
2013: NOTE: `email.body.to_s` is present when there's only one (HTML or text) part present. If the mailer provides both, you can test your fixture against specific parts with `email.text_part.body.to_s` or `email.html_part.body.to_s`.
2014: 
2015: Here's the content of the `invite` fixture:
2016: 
2017: ```
2018: Hi friend@example.com,
2019: 
2020: You have been invited.
2021: 
2022: Cheers!
2023: ```
2024: 
2025: This is the right time to understand a little more about writing tests for your mailers. The line `ActionMailer::Base.delivery_method = :test` in `config/environments/test.rb` sets the delivery method to test mode so that email will not actually be delivered (useful to avoid spamming your users while testing) but instead it will be appended to an array (`ActionMailer::Base.deliveries`).
2026: 
2027: NOTE: The `ActionMailer::Base.deliveries` array is only reset automatically in `ActionMailer::TestCase` and `ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest` tests. If you want to have a clean slate outside these test cases, you can reset it manually with: `ActionMailer::Base.deliveries.clear`
2028: 
2029: #### Testing Enqueued Emails
2030: 
2031: You can use the `assert_enqueued_email_with` assertion to confirm that the email has been enqueued with all of the expected mailer method arguments and/or parameterized mailer parameters. This allows you to match any email that have been enqueued with the `deliver_later` method.
2032: 
2033: As with the basic test case, we create the email and store the returned object in the `email` variable. The following examples include variations of passing arguments and/or parameters.
2034: 
2035: This example will assert that the email has been enqueued with the correct arguments:
2036: 
2037: ```ruby
2038: require "test_helper"
2039: 
2040: class UserMailerTest < ActionMailer::TestCase
2041:   test "invite" do
2042:     # Create the email and store it for further assertions
2043:     email = UserMailer.create_invite("me@example.com", "friend@example.com")
2044: 
2045:     # Test that the email got enqueued with the correct arguments
2046:     assert_enqueued_email_with UserMailer, :create_invite, args: ["me@example.com", "friend@example.com"] do
2047:       email.deliver_later
2048:     end
2049:   end
2050: end
2051: ```
2052: 
2053: This example will assert that a mailer has been enqueued with the correct mailer method named arguments by passing a hash of the arguments as `args`:
2054: 
2055: ```ruby
2056: require "test_helper"
2057: 
2058: class UserMailerTest < ActionMailer::TestCase
2059:   test "invite" do
2060:     # Create the email and store it for further assertions
2061:     email = UserMailer.create_invite(from: "me@example.com", to: "friend@example.com")
2062: 
2063:     # Test that the email got enqueued with the correct named arguments
2064:     assert_enqueued_email_with UserMailer, :create_invite, args: [{ from: "me@example.com",
2065:                                                                     to: "friend@example.com" }] do
2066:       email.deliver_later
2067:     end
2068:   end
2069: end
2070: ```

**DO NOT READ THIS FILE ON GITHUB, GUIDES ARE PUBLISHED ON https://guides.rubyonrails.org.** Action Mailer Basics ==================== This guide provides you with all you need to get started in sending emails from your application, and many internals of Action Mailer. It also covers how to test your mailers. After reading this guide, you will know: * How to send email within a Rails application. * How to generate and edit an Action Mailer class and mailer view. * How to configure Action Mailer for your environment. * How to test your Action Mailer classes. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- What is Action Mailer? ---------------------- Action Mailer allows you to send emails from your application using mailer classes and views. ### Mailers are Similar to Controllers They inherit from [`ActionMailer::Base`][] and live in `app/mailers`. Mailers also work very similarly to controllers. Some examples of similarities are enumerated below. Mailers have: * Actions, and also, associated views that appear in `app/views`. * Instance variables that are accessible in views. * The ability to utilise layouts and partials. * The ability to access a params hash. [`ActionMailer::Base`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html Sending Emails -------------- This section will provide a step-by-step guide to creating a mailer and its views. ### Walkthrough to Generating a Mailer #### Create the Mailer ```bash $ bin/rails generate mailer User create app/mailers/user_mailer.rb create app/mailers/application_mailer.rb invoke erb create app/views/user_mailer create app/views/layouts/mailer.text.erb create app/views/layouts/mailer.html.erb invoke test_unit create test/mailers/user_mailer_test.rb create test/mailers/previews/user_mailer_preview.rb ``` ```ruby # app/mailers/application_mailer.rb class ApplicationMailer < ActionMailer::Base default from: "from@example.com" layout "mailer" end ``` ```ruby # app/mailers/user_mailer.rb class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer end ``` As you can see, you can generate mailers just like you use other generators with Rails. If you didn't want to use a generator, you could create your own file inside of `app/mailers`, just make sure that it inherits from `ActionMailer::Base`: ```ruby class MyMailer < ActionMailer::Base end ``` #### Edit the Mailer Mailers have methods called "actions" and they use views to structure their content. Where a controller generates content like HTML to send back to the client, a Mailer creates a message to be delivered via email. `app/mailers/user_mailer.rb` contains an empty mailer: ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer end ``` Let's add a method called `welcome_email`, that will send an email to the user's registered email address: ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer default from: 'notifications@example.com' def welcome_email @user = params[:user] @url = 'http://example.com/login' mail(to: @user.email, subject: 'Welcome to My Awesome Site') end end ``` Here is a quick explanation of the items presented in the preceding method. For a full list of all available options, please have a look further down at the [Complete List of Action Mailer Methods](#complete-list-of-action-mailer-methods) section. * The [`default`][] method sets default values for all emails sent from this mailer. In this case, we use it to set the `:from` header value for all messages in this class. This can be overridden on a per-email basis. * The [`mail`][] method creates the actual email message. We use it to specify the values of headers like `:to` and `:subject` per email. [`default`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-c-default [`mail`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-mail #### Create a Mailer View Create a file called `welcome_email.html.erb` in `app/views/user_mailer/`. This will be the template used for the email, formatted in HTML: ```html+erb

Welcome to example.com, <%= @user.name %>

You have successfully signed up to example.com, your username is: <%= @user.login %>.

To login to the site, just follow this link: <%= @url %>.

Thanks for joining and have a great day!

``` The template above only contains the content of the email. The surrounding ``, ``, and `` tags are provided by the `mailer` layout, which is applied to every email because the generated `ApplicationMailer` calls [`layout 'mailer'`][layout]. The layout is created by the generator: ```html+erb <%= yield %> ``` There is also a plain text layout, which simply renders the content of the view: ```erb <%= yield %> ``` Let's also make a text part for this email. Not all email clients prefer HTML emails, and so sending both is best practice. To do this, create a file called `welcome_email.text.erb` in `app/views/user_mailer/`: ```erb Welcome to example.com, <%= @user.name %> =============================================== You have successfully signed up to example.com, your username is: <%= @user.login %>. To login to the site, just follow this link: <%= @url %>. Thanks for joining and have a great day! ``` When you call the `mail` method now, Action Mailer will detect the two templates (text and HTML) and automatically generate a `multipart/alternative` email. See the [Sending Multipart Emails](#sending-multipart-emails) section below for more details on the benefits of sending multipart emails. [layout]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/Layouts/ClassMethods.html#method-i-layout #### Calling the Mailer Mailers are really just another way to render a view. Instead of rendering a view and sending it over the HTTP protocol, they are sending it out through the email protocols instead. Due to this, it makes sense to have your controller tell the Mailer to send an email when a user is successfully created. Setting this up is simple. First, let's create a `User` scaffold: ```bash $ bin/rails generate scaffold user name email login $ bin/rails db:migrate ``` Now that we have a user model to play with, we will edit the `app/controllers/users_controller.rb` file, make it instruct the `UserMailer` to deliver an email to the newly created user by editing the create action and inserting a call to `UserMailer.with(user: @user).welcome_email` right after the user is successfully saved. We will enqueue the email to be sent by using [`deliver_later`][], which is backed by Active Job. That way, the controller action can continue without waiting for the send to complete. ```ruby class UsersController < ApplicationController # ... # POST /users or /users.json def create @user = User.new(user_params) if @user.save # Tell the UserMailer to send a welcome email after save UserMailer.with(user: @user).welcome_email.deliver_later redirect_to(@user, notice: "User was successfully created.") else render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity end end # ... end ``` NOTE: Active Job's default behavior is to execute jobs via the `:async` adapter. So, you can use `deliver_later` to send emails asynchronously. Active Job's default adapter runs jobs with an in-process thread pool. It's well-suited for the development/test environments, since it doesn't require any external infrastructure, but it's a poor fit for production since it drops pending jobs on restart. If you need a persistent backend, you will need to use an Active Job adapter that has a persistent backend (Sidekiq, Resque, etc). Read more about background jobs in the [Active Job Basics](active_job_basics.html) guide. If you want to send emails right away (from a cronjob for example) just call [`deliver_now`][]: ```ruby class SendWeeklySummary def run User.find_each do |user| UserMailer.with(user: user).weekly_summary.deliver_now end end end ``` Any key-value pair passed to [`with`][] just becomes the `params` for the mailer action. So `with(user: @user, account: @user.account)` makes `params[:user]` and `params[:account]` available in the mailer action. Just like controllers have params. The method `weekly_summary` returns an [`ActionMailer::MessageDelivery`][] object which can then be told to `deliver_now` or `deliver_later` to send itself out. The `ActionMailer::MessageDelivery` object is a wrapper around a [`Mail::Message`][]. If you want to inspect, alter, or do anything else with the `Mail::Message` object you can access it with the [`message`][] method on the `ActionMailer::MessageDelivery` object. [`ActionMailer::MessageDelivery`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html [`deliver_later`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html#method-i-deliver_later [`deliver_now`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html#method-i-deliver_now [`Mail::Message`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Mail/Message.html [`message`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/MessageDelivery.html#method-i-message [`with`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Parameterized/ClassMethods.html#method-i-with ### Auto Encoding Header Values Action Mailer handles the auto encoding of multibyte characters inside of headers and bodies. For more complex examples such as defining alternate character sets or self-encoding text first, please refer to the [Mail](https://github.com/mikel/mail) library. ### Complete List of Action Mailer Methods There are just three methods that you need to send pretty much any email message: * [`headers`][] - Specifies any header on the email you want. You can pass a hash of header field names and value pairs, or you can call `headers[:field_name] = 'value'`. * [`attachments`][] - Allows you to add attachments to your email. For example, `attachments['file-name.jpg'] = File.read('file-name.jpg')`. * [`mail`][] - Creates the actual email itself. You can pass in headers as a hash to the `mail` method as a parameter. `mail` will create an email — either plain text or multipart — depending on what email templates you have defined. [`attachments`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-attachments [`headers`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-headers #### Adding Attachments Action Mailer makes it very easy to add attachments. * Pass the file name and content and Action Mailer and the [Mail gem](https://github.com/mikel/mail) will automatically guess the `mime_type`, set the `encoding`, and create the attachment. ```ruby attachments['filename.jpg'] = File.read('/path/to/filename.jpg') ``` When the `mail` method will be triggered, it will send a multipart email with an attachment, properly nested with the top level being `multipart/mixed` and the first part being a `multipart/alternative` containing the plain text and HTML email messages. NOTE: Mail will automatically Base64 encode an attachment. If you want something different, encode your content and pass in the encoded content and encoding in a `Hash` to the `attachments` method. * Pass the file name and specify headers and content and Action Mailer and Mail will use the settings you pass in. ```ruby encoded_content = SpecialEncode(File.read('/path/to/filename.jpg')) attachments['filename.jpg'] = { mime_type: 'application/gzip', encoding: 'SpecialEncoding', content: encoded_content } ``` NOTE: If you specify an encoding, Mail will assume that your content is already encoded and not try to Base64 encode it. #### Making Inline Attachments Action Mailer offers a simpler and trivial way to make inline attachments. * First, to tell Mail to turn an attachment into an inline attachment, you just call `#inline` on the attachments method within your Mailer: ```ruby def welcome attachments.inline['image.jpg'] = File.read('/path/to/image.jpg') end ``` * Then in your view, you can just reference `attachments` as a hash and specify which attachment you want to show, calling `url` on it and then passing the result into the `image_tag` method: ```html+erb

Hello there, this is our image

<%= image_tag attachments['image.jpg'].url %> ``` * As this is a standard call to `image_tag` you can pass in an options hash after the attachment URL as you could for any other image: ```html+erb

Hello there, this is our image

<%= image_tag attachments['image.jpg'].url, alt: 'My Photo', class: 'photos' %> ``` #### Sending Email to Multiple Recipients It is possible to send email to one or more recipients in one email (e.g., informing all admins of a new signup) by setting the list of emails to the `:to` key. The list of emails can be an array of email addresses or a single string with the addresses separated by commas. ```ruby class AdminMailer < ApplicationMailer default to: -> { Admin.pluck(:email) }, from: 'notification@example.com' def new_registration(user) @user = user mail(subject: "New User Signup: #{@user.email}") end end ``` The same format can be used to set carbon copy (Cc:) and blind carbon copy (Bcc:) recipients, by using the `:cc` and `:bcc` keys respectively. #### Sending Email with Name Sometimes you wish to show the name of the person instead of just their email address when they receive the email. You can also specify an array of paths for `template_path`, and they will be searched in order. The render command is the same one used inside of Action Controller, so you can use all the same options, such as `:text`, `:inline`, etc. If you would like to render a template located outside of the default `app/views/mailer_name/` directory, you can apply the [`prepend_view_path`][], like so: ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer prepend_view_path "custom/path/to/mailer/view" # This will try to load "custom/path/to/mailer/view/welcome_email" template def welcome_email # ... end end ``` You can also consider using the [`append_view_path`][] method. [`append_view_path`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/ViewPaths/ClassMethods.html#method-i-append_view_path [`prepend_view_path`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/ViewPaths/ClassMethods.html#method-i-prepend_view_path #### Caching Mailer View You can perform fragment caching in mailer views like in application views using the [`cache`][] method. ```html+erb <% cache do %> <%= @company.name %> <% end %> ``` And to use this feature, you need to configure your application with this: ```ruby config.action_mailer.perform_caching = true ``` Fragment caching is also supported in multipart emails. Read more about caching in the [Rails caching guide](caching_with_rails.html). [`cache`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/Helpers/CacheHelper.html#method-i-cache ### Action Mailer Layouts Just like controller views, you can also have mailer layouts. The layout name needs to be the same as your mailer, such as `user_mailer.html.erb` and `user_mailer.text.erb` to be automatically recognized by your mailer as a layout. To use a different file, call [`layout`][] in your mailer: ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer layout 'awesome' # use awesome.(html|text).erb as the layout end ``` Just like with controller views, use `yield` to render the view inside the layout. [`layout`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/Layouts/ClassMethods.html#method-i-layout ### Previewing Emails Action Mailer previews provide a way to see how emails look by visiting a special URL that renders them. To see the preview of `welcome_email`, implement a method that has the same name and call `UserMailer.welcome_email`: ```ruby class UserMailerPreview < ActionMailer::Preview def welcome_email UserMailer.with(user: User.first).welcome_email end end ``` Then the preview will be available in . If you change something in `app/views/user_mailer/welcome_email.html.erb` or the mailer itself, it'll automatically reload and render it so you can visually see the new style instantly. For example, if you want to add `lib/mailer_previews` to it, you can configure it in `config/application.rb`: ```ruby config.action_mailer.preview_paths << "#{Rails.root}/lib/mailer_previews" ``` ### Generating URLs in Action Mailer Views Unlike controllers, the mailer instance doesn't have any context about the incoming request so you'll need to provide the `:host` parameter yourself. As the `:host` usually is consistent across the application you can configure it globally in `config/application.rb`: ```ruby config.action_mailer.default_url_options = { host: 'example.com' } ``` Because of this behavior, you cannot use any of the `*_path` helpers inside of an email. Instead, you will need to use the associated `*_url` helper. For example instead of using ```html+erb <%= link_to 'welcome', welcome_path %> ``` You will need to use: ```html+erb <%= link_to 'welcome', welcome_url %> ``` By using the full URL, your links will now work in your emails. #### Generating URLs with `url_for` [`url_for`][] generates a full URL by default in templates. If you did not configure the `:host` option globally make sure to pass it to `url_for`. ```erb <%= url_for(host: 'example.com', controller: 'welcome', action: 'greeting') %> ``` [`url_for`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionView/RoutingUrlFor.html#method-i-url_for #### Generating URLs with Named Routes Email clients have no web context and so paths have no base URL to form complete web addresses. Thus, you should always use the `*_url` variant of named route helpers. If you did not configure the `:host` option globally make sure to pass it to the URL helper. ```erb <%= user_url(@user, host: 'example.com') %> ``` ### Adding Images in Action Mailer Views Unlike controllers, the mailer instance doesn't have any context about the incoming request so you'll need to provide the `:asset_host` parameter yourself. As the `:asset_host` usually is consistent across the application you can configure it globally in `config/application.rb`: ```ruby config.action_mailer.asset_host = 'http://example.com' ``` NOTE: Because we can't infer the protocol from the request, you'll need to specify a protocol such as `http://` or `https://` in the `:asset_host` config. So, for our `UserMailer` example, if you have `welcome_email.text.erb` and `welcome_email.html.erb` in `app/views/user_mailer`, Action Mailer will automatically send a multipart email with the HTML and text versions set up as different parts. Sending both parts has several benefits: * Email clients that do not support HTML will render the plain text part, so everyone gets a readable version of your email. * HTML parts can use richer formatting, such as links, images, and layout, while the plain text part keeps the email accessible to screen readers and other assistive technology. * Including a plain text alternative improves deliverability, since some spam filters treat HTML-only emails with suspicion. The performed lookup will use the pattern `..subject` to construct the key. ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer def welcome_email @user = params[:user] mail(to: @user.email) end end ``` ```yaml # config/locales/en.yml en: user_mailer: welcome_email: subject: "Welcome to My Awesome Site" ``` To pass parameters to the subject, use the [`default_i18n_subject`][] method: ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer def welcome_email @user = params[:user] mail(to: @user.email, subject: default_i18n_subject(name: @user.name)) end end ``` ```yaml en: user_mailer: welcome_email: subject: "Welcome to My Awesome Site, %{name}!" ``` Since a subject that evaluates to `nil` also triggers the lookup, you can add localization to an existing mailer without changing it, by removing the `subject` option just as shown above. You can read more about the [Translations for Action Mailer E-Mail Subjects](i18n.html#translations-for-action-mailer-e-mail-subjects) in the I18n guide. For example, a record referenced by the mailer action may have been deleted, or the SMTP server may be unreachable. These errors can be handled with [`rescue_from`][], which works in mailers exactly like it does in controllers. Handlers are invoked both when the error is raised while the mailer action is being processed, and when it is raised during delivery (with either `deliver_now` or `deliver_later`). ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound do |exception| logger.error "Unable to send email: #{exception.message}" end end ``` [`rescue_from`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveSupport/Rescuable/ClassMethods.html#method-i-rescue_from Action Mailer Callbacks ----------------------- Action Mailer allows for you to specify a can be specified with a block or a symbol to a method in the mailer class similar to controllers. * You could use a `before_action` to set instance variables, populate the mail object with defaults, or insert default headers and attachments. ```ruby class InvitationsMailer < ApplicationMailer before_action :set_inviter_and_invitee before_action { @account = params[:inviter].account } default to: -> { @invitee.email_address }, from: -> { common_address(@inviter) }, reply_to: -> { @inviter.email_address_with_name } def account_invitation mail subject: "#{@inviter.name} invited you to their Basecamp (#{@account.name})" end def project_invitation @project = params[:project] @summarizer = ProjectInvitationSummarizer.new(@project.bucket) mail subject: "#{@inviter.name.familiar} added you to a project in Basecamp (#{@account.name})" end private def set_inviter_and_invitee @inviter = params[:inviter] @invitee = params[:invitee] end end ``` * You could use an `after_action` to do similar setup as a `before_action` but using instance variables set in your mailer action. * Using an `after_action` callback also enables you to override delivery method settings by updating `mail.delivery_method.settings`. ```ruby class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer before_action { @business, @user = params[:business], params[:user] } after_action :set_delivery_options, :prevent_delivery_to_guests, :set_business_headers def feedback_message end def campaign_message end private def set_delivery_options # You have access to the mail instance, # @business and @user instance variables here if @business && @business.has_smtp_settings? mail.delivery_method.settings.merge!(@business.smtp_settings) end end def prevent_delivery_to_guests if @user && @user.guest? mail.perform_deliveries = false end end def set_business_headers if @business headers["X-SMTPAPI-CATEGORY"] = @business.code end end end ``` * You could use an `after_deliver` to record the delivery 198: #### Calling the Mailer
199: 
200: Mailers are really just another way to render a view. Instead of rendering a
201: view and sending it over the HTTP protocol, they are sending it out through
202: the email protocols instead. Due to this, it makes sense to have your
203: controller tell the Mailer to send an email when a user is successfully created.
204: 
205: Setting this up is simple.
206: 
207: First, let's create a `User` scaffold:
208: 
209: ```bash
210: $ bin/rails generate scaffold user name email login
211: $ bin/rails db:migrate
212: ```
213: 
214: Now that we have a user model to play with, we will edit the
215: `app/controllers/users_controller.rb` file, make it instruct the `UserMailer` to deliver
216: an email to the newly created user by editing the create action and inserting a
217: call to `UserMailer.with(user: @user).welcome_email` right after the user is successfully saved.
218: 
219: We will enqueue the email to be sent by using [`deliver_later`][], which is
220: backed by Active Job. That way, the controller action can continue without
221: waiting for the send to complete.
222: 
223: ```ruby
224: class UsersController < ApplicationController
225:   # ...
226: 
227:   # POST /users or /users.json
228:   def create
229:     @user = User.new(user_params)
230: 
231:     if @user.save
232:       # Tell the UserMailer to send a welcome email after save
233:       UserMailer.with(user: @user).welcome_email.deliver_later
234: 
235:       redirect_to(@user, notice: "User was successfully created.")
236:     else
237:       render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity
238:     end
239:   end
240: 
241:   # ...
242: end
243: ```
244: 
245: NOTE: Active Job's default behavior is to execute jobs via the `:async` adapter.
246: So, you can use `deliver_later` to send emails asynchronously.
247: Active Job's default adapter runs jobs with an in-process thread pool.
248: It's well-suited for the development/test environments, since it doesn't require
249: any external infrastructure, but it's a poor fit for production since it drops
250: pending jobs on restart.
251: If you need a persistent backend, you will need to use an Active Job adapter
252: that has a persistent backend (Sidekiq, Resque, etc).
253: Read more about background jobs in the [Active Job Basics](active_job_basics.html)
254: guide.
255: 
256: If you want to send emails right away (from a cronjob for example) just call
257: [`deliver_now`][]:
258: 
259: ```ruby
260: class SendWeeklySummary
261:   def run
262:     User.find_each do |user|
263:       UserMailer.with(user: user).weekly_summary.deliver_now
264:     end
265:   end
266: end
267: ```
268: 
269: Any key-value pair passed to [`with`][] just becomes the `params` for the mailer
270: action. So `with(user: @user, account: @user.account)` makes `params[:user]` and
271: `params[:account]` available in the mailer action. Just like controllers have
272: params.
273: 
274: The method `weekly_summary` returns an [`ActionMailer::MessageDelivery`][] object which
275: can then be told to `deliver_now` or `deliver_later` to send itself out. The
276: `ActionMailer::MessageDelivery` object is a wrapper around a [`Mail::Message`][]. If
277: you want to inspect, alter, or do anything else with the `Mail::Message` object you can
278: access it with the [`message`][] method on the `ActionMailer::MessageDelivery` object.
279:

287: ### Auto Encoding Header Values
288: 
289: Action Mailer handles the auto encoding of multibyte characters inside of
290: headers and bodies.
291: 
292: For more complex examples such as defining alternate character sets or
293: self-encoding text first, please refer to the
294: [Mail](https://github.com/mikel/mail) library.
295: 
296: ### Complete List of Action Mailer Methods
297: 
298: There are just three methods that you need to send pretty much any email
299: message:
300: 
301: * [`headers`][] - Specifies any header on the email you want. You can pass a hash of
302:   header field names and value pairs, or you can call `headers[:field_name] =
303:   'value'`.
304: * [`attachments`][] - Allows you to add attachments to your email. For example,
305:   `attachments['file-name.jpg'] = File.read('file-name.jpg')`.
306: * [`mail`][] - Creates the actual email itself. You can pass in headers as a hash to
307:   the `mail` method as a parameter. `mail` will create an email — either plain
308:   text or multipart — depending on what email templates you have defined.
309: 
310: [`attachments`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActionMailer/Base.html#method-i-attachments

649: ### Adding Images in Action Mailer Views

651: Unlike controllers, the mailer instance doesn't have any context about the

653:

663: `:asset_host` config.
664: 
665: Now you can display an image inside your email.
666:

671: ### Sending Multipart Emails
672: 
673: Action Mailer will automatically send multipart emails if you have different
674: templates for the same action. So, for our `UserMailer` example, if you have
675: `welcome_email.text.erb` and `welcome_email.html.erb` in
676: `app/views/user_mailer`, Action Mailer will automatically send a multipart email
677: with the HTML and text versions set up as different parts.
678: 
679: Sending both parts has several benefits:
680: 
681: * Email clients that do not support HTML will render the plain text part, so
682:   everyone gets a readable version of your email.
683: * HTML parts can use richer formatting, such as links, images, and layout, while
684:   the plain text part keeps the email accessible to screen readers and other
685:   assistive technology.
686: * Including a plain text alternative improves deliverability, since some spam
687:   filters treat HTML-only emails with suspicion.
688: 
689: The order of the parts getting inserted is determined by the `:parts_order`
690: inside of the `ActionMailer::Base.default` method.
691: 
692: ### Sending Emails with Dynamic Delivery Options
693: 
694: If you wish to override the default delivery options (e.g. SMTP credentials)
695: while delivering emails, you can do this using `delivery_method_options` in the
696: mailer action.
697: 
698: ```ruby
699: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer
700:   def welcome_email
701:     @user = params[:user]
702:     @url  = user_url(@user)
703:     delivery_options = { user_name: params[:company].smtp_user,
704:                          password: params[:company].smtp_password,
705:                          address: params[:company].smtp_host }
706:     mail(to: @user.email,
707:          subject: "Please see the Terms and Conditions attached",
708:          delivery_method_options: delivery_options)
709:   end
710: end
711: ```
712: 
713: ### Sending Emails without Template Rendering
714: 
715: There may be cases in which you want to skip the template rendering step and
716: supply the email body as a string. You can achieve this using the `:body`
717: option. In such cases don't forget to add the `:content_type` option. Rails
718: will default to `text/plain` otherwise.
719: 
720: ```ruby
721: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer
722:   def welcome_email
723:     mail(to: params[:user].email,
724:          body: params[:email_body],
725:          content_type: "text/html",
726:          subject: "Already rendered!")
727:   end
728: end
729: ```

731: ### Sending Emails with Internationalization (I18n)
732: 
733: The subject of an email can be localized using the
734: [Rails Internationalization (I18n) API](i18n.html). When you don't pass a
735: `subject` to the [`mail`][] method, Action Mailer will try to find it in your
736: translations. The performed lookup will use the pattern
737: `<mailer_scope>.<action_name>.subject` to construct the key.
738: 
739: ```ruby
740: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer
741:   def welcome_email
742:     @user = params[:user]
743:     mail(to: @user.email)
744:   end
745: end
746: ```
747: 
748: ```yaml
749: # config/locales/en.yml
750: en:
751:   user_mailer:
752:     welcome_email:
753:       subject: "Welcome to My Awesome Site"
754: ```
755: 
756: To pass parameters to the subject, use the [`default_i18n_subject`][] method:
757: 
758: ```ruby
759: class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer
760:   def welcome_email
761:     @user = params[:user]
762:     mail(to: @user.email, subject: default_i18n_subject(name: @user.name))
763:   end
764: end
765: ```
766: 
767: ```yaml
768: en:
769:   user_mailer:
770:     welcome_email:
771:       subject: "Welcome to My Awesome Site, %{name}!"
772: ```
773: 
774: Setting the subject to `nil` also triggers the lookup, so you can
775: internationalize an existing mailer simply by removing its `subject` option, as
776: shown above.
777: 
778: You can read more about the

3: Active Record Validations
4: =========================
5: 
6: This guide teaches you how to validate the state of objects before they go into
7: the database using Active Record's validations feature.
8: 
9: After reading this guide, you will know:
10: 
11: * How to use the built-in Active Record validation helpers.
12: * How to create your own custom validation methods.
13: * How to work with the error messages generated by the validation process.
14: 
15: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
16: 
17: Validations Overview
18: --------------------
19: 
20: Here's an example of a very simple validation:
21: 
22: ```ruby
23: class Person < ApplicationRecord
24:   validates :name, presence: true
25: end
26: ```
27: 
28: ```irb
29: irb> Person.create(name: "John Doe").valid?
30: => true
31: irb> Person.create(name: nil).valid?
32: => false
33: ```
34: 
35: As you can see, our validation lets us know that our `Person` is not valid
36: without a `name` attribute. The second `Person` will not be persisted to the
37: database.
38: 
39: Before we dig into more details, let's talk about how validations fit into the
40: big picture of your application.
41: 
42: ### Why Use Validations?
43: 
44: Validations are used to ensure that only valid data is saved into your
45: database. For example, it may be important to your application to ensure that
46: every user provides a valid email address and mailing address. Model-level
47: validations are the best way to ensure that only valid data is saved into your
48: database. They are database agnostic, cannot be bypassed by end users, and are
49: convenient to test and maintain. Rails provides built-in helpers for common
50: needs, and allows you to create your own validation methods as well.
51: 
52: There are several other ways to validate data before it is saved into your
53: database, including native database constraints, client-side validations and
54: controller-level validations. Here's a summary of the pros and cons:
55: 
56: * Database constraints and/or stored procedures make the validation mechanisms
57:   database-dependent and can make testing and maintenance more difficult.
58:   However, if your database is used by other applications, it may be a good
59:   idea to use some constraints at the database level. Additionally,
60:   database-level validations can safely handle some things (such as uniqueness
61:   in heavily-used tables) that can be difficult to implement otherwise.
62: * Client-side validations can be useful, but are generally unreliable if used
63:   alone. If they are implemented using JavaScript, they may be bypassed if
64:   JavaScript is turned off in the user's browser. However, if combined with
65:   other techniques, client-side validation can be a convenient way to provide
66:   users with immediate feedback as they use your site.
67: * Controller-level validations can be tempting to use, but often become
68:   unwieldy and difficult to test and maintain. Whenever possible, it's a good
69:   idea to keep your controllers simple, as it will make your
70:   application a pleasure to work with in the long run.
71: 
72: Choose these in certain, specific cases. It's the opinion of the Rails team
73: that model-level validations are the most appropriate in most circumstances.
74: 
75: ### When Does Validation Happen?
76: 
77: There are two kinds of Active Record objects: those that correspond to a row
78: inside your database and those that do not. When you create a fresh object, for
79: example using the `new` method, that object does not belong to the database
80: yet. Once you call `save` upon that object it will be saved into the
81: appropriate database table. Active Record uses the `new_record?` instance
82: method to determine whether an object is already in the database or not.
83: Consider the following Active Record class:
84: 
85: ```ruby
86: class Person < ApplicationRecord
87: end
88: ```
89: 
90: We can see how it works by looking at some `bin/rails console` output:
91: 
92: ```irb
93: irb> p = Person.new(name: "John Doe")
94: => #<Person id: nil, name: "John Doe", created_at: nil, updated_at: nil>
95: 
96: irb> p.new_record?
97: => true
98: 
99: irb> p.save
100: => true
101: 
102: irb> p.new_record?
103: => false
104: ```
105: 
106: Creating and saving a new record will send an SQL `INSERT` operation to the
107: database. Updating an existing record will send an SQL `UPDATE` operation
108: instead. Validations are typically run before these commands are sent to the
109: database. If any validations fail, the object will be marked as invalid and
110: Active Record will not perform the `INSERT` or `UPDATE` operation. This avoids
111: storing an invalid object in the database. You can choose to have specific
112: validations run when an object is created, saved, or updated.
113: 
114: CAUTION: There are many ways to change the state of an object in the database.
115: Some methods will trigger validations, but some will not. This means that it's
116: possible to save an object in the database in an invalid state if you aren't
117: careful.
118: 
119: The following methods trigger validations, and will save the object to the
120: database only if the object is valid:
121: 
122: * [`create`][]
123: * [`create!`][]
124: * [`save`][]
125: * [`save!`][]
126: * [`update`][]
127: * [`update!`][]
128: 
129: The bang versions (e.g. `save!`) raise an exception if the record is invalid.
130: The non-bang versions don't: `save` and `update` return `false`, and
131: `create` returns the object.
132:
