191: ### `valid?` and `invalid?`
192: 
193: Before saving an Active Record object, Rails runs your validations.
194: If these validations produce any errors, Rails does not save the object.
195: 
196: You can also run these validations on your own. [`valid?`][] triggers your validations
197: and returns true if no errors were found in the object, and false otherwise.
198: As you saw above:
199: 
200: ```ruby
201: class Person < ApplicationRecord
202:   validates :name, presence: true
203: end
204: ```
205: 
206: ```irb
207: irb> Person.create(name: "John Doe").valid?
208: => true
209: irb> Person.create(name: nil).valid?
210: => false
211: ```
212: 
213: After Active Record has performed validations, any failures can be accessed
214: through the [`errors`][] instance method, which returns a collection of errors.
215: By definition, an object is valid if this collection is empty after running
216: validations.
217: 
218: Note that an object instantiated with `new` will not report errors
219: even if it's technically invalid, because validations are automatically run
220: only when the object is saved, such as with the `create` or `save` methods.
221: 
222: ```ruby
223: class Person < ApplicationRecord
224:   validates :name, presence: true
225: end
226: ```
227: 
228: ```irb
229: irb> p = Person.new
230: => #<Person id: nil, name: nil>
231: irb> p.errors.size
232: => 0
233: 
234: irb> p.valid?
235: => false
236: irb> p.errors.objects.first.full_message
237: => "Name can't be blank"
238: 
239: irb> p = Person.create
240: => #<Person id: nil, name: nil>
241: irb> p.errors.objects.first.full_message
242: => "Name can't be blank"
243: 
244: irb> p.save
245: => false
246: 
247: irb> p.save!
248: ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid: Validation failed: Name can't be blank
249: 
250: irb> Person.create!
251: ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid: Validation failed: Name can't be blank
252: ```
253: 
254: [`invalid?`][] is the inverse of `valid?`. It triggers your validations,
255: returning true if any errors were found in the object, and false otherwise.
256: 
257: [`errors`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validations.html#method-i-errors
258: [`invalid?`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validations.html#method-i-invalid-3F
259: [`valid?`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/Validations.html#method-i-valid-3F
260: 
261: ### `errors[]`
262: 
263: To verify whether or not a particular attribute of an object is valid, you can
264: use [`errors[:attribute]`][Errors#squarebrackets]. It returns an array of all
265: the error messages for `:attribute`. If there are no errors on the specified
266: attribute, an empty array is returned.
267: 
268: This method is only useful _after_ validations have been run, because it only
269: inspects the errors collection and does not trigger validations itself. It's
270: different from the `ActiveRecord::Base#invalid?` method explained above because
271: it doesn't verify the validity of the object as a whole. It only checks to see
272: whether there are errors found on an individual attribute of the object.
273: 
274: ```ruby
275: class Person < ApplicationRecord
276:   validates :name, presence: true
277: end
278: ```
279: 
280: ```irb
281: irb> Person.new.errors[:name].any?
282: => false
283: irb> Person.create.errors[:name].any?
284: => true
285: ```
286: 
287: We'll cover validation errors in greater depth in the [Working with Validation
288: Errors](#working-with-validation-errors) section.
289: 
290: [Errors#squarebrackets]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Errors.html#method-i-5B-5D
291: 
292: Validation Helpers
293: ------------------
294: 
295: Active Record offers many pre-defined validation helpers that you can use
296: directly inside your class definitions. These helpers provide common validation
297: rules. Every time a validation fails, an error is added to the object's `errors`
298: collection, and this is associated with the attribute being validated.
299: 
300: Each helper accepts an arbitrary number of attribute names, so with a single
301: line of code you can add the same kind of validation to several attributes.
302: 
303: All of them accept the `:on` and `:message` options, which define when the
304: validation should be run and what message should be added to the `errors`
305: collection if it fails, respectively. The `:on` option takes one of the values
306: `:create` or `:update`. There is a default error message for each one of the
307: validation helpers. These messages are used when the `:message` option isn't
308: specified. Let's take a look at each one of the available helpers.
309: 
310: INFO: To see a list of the available default helpers, take a look at
311: [`ActiveModel::Validations::HelperMethods`][].
312: 
313: [`ActiveModel::Validations::HelperMethods`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validations/HelperMethods.html
314: 
315: ### `acceptance`
316: 
317: This method validates that a checkbox on the user interface was checked when a
318: form was submitted. This is typically used when the user needs to agree to your
319: application's terms of service, confirm that some text is read, or any similar
320: concept.
321: 
322: ```ruby
323: class Person < ApplicationRecord
324:   validates :terms_of_service, acceptance: true
325: end
326: ```
327: 
328: This check is performed only if `terms_of_service` is not `nil`.
329: The default error message for this helper is _"must be accepted"_.
330: You can also pass in a custom message via the `message` option.
331: 
332: ```ruby
333: class Person < ApplicationRecord
334:   validates :terms_of_service, acceptance: { message: 'must be abided' }
335: end
336: ```
337: 
338: It can also receive an `:accept` option, which determines the allowed values
339: that will be considered as acceptable. It defaults to `['1', true]` and can be
340: easily changed.
341: 
342: ```ruby
343: class Person < ApplicationRecord
344:   validates :terms_of_service, acceptance: { accept: 'yes' }
345:   validates :eula, acceptance: { accept: ['TRUE', 'accepted'] }
346: end
347: ```
348: 
349: This validation is very specific to web applications and this 'acceptance' does
350: not need to be recorded anywhere in your database. If you don't have a field for
351: it, the helper will create a virtual attribute. If the field does exist in your
352: database, the `accept` option must be set to or include `true` or else the
353: validation will not run.
354: 
355: ### `confirmation`
356: 
357: You should use this helper when you have two text fields that should receive
358: exactly the same content. For example, you may want to confirm an email address
359: or a password. This validation creates a virtual attribute whose name is the
360: name of the field that has to be confirmed with "_confirmation" appended.
361: 
362: ```ruby
363: class Person < ApplicationRecord
364:   validates :email, confirmation: true
365: end
366: ```
367: 
368: In your view template you could use something like
369: 
370: ```erb
371: <%= text_field :person, :email %>
372: <%= text_field :person, :email_confirmation %>
373: ```
374: 
375: NOTE: This check is performed only if `email_confirmation` is not `nil`. To require
376: confirmation, make sure to add a presence check for the confirmation attribute
377: (we'll take a look at `presence` [later](#presence) on in this guide):
378: 
379: ```ruby
380: class Person < ApplicationRecord
381:   validates :email, confirmation: true
382:   validates :email_confirmation, presence: true
383: end
384: ```
385: 
386: There is also a `:case_sensitive` option that you can use to define whether the
387: confirmation constraint will be case sensitive or not. This option defaults to
388: true.
389: 
390: ```ruby
391: class Person < ApplicationRecord
392:   validates :email, confirmation: { case_sensitive: false }
393: end
394: ```
395: 
396: The default error message for this helper is _"doesn't match confirmation"_.
397: You can also pass in a custom message via the `message` option.
398: 
399: Generally when using this validator, you will want to combine it with the `:if`
400: option to only validate the "_confirmation" field when the initial field has
401: changed and **not** every time you save the record. More on [conditional
402: validations](#conditional-validation) later.
403: 
404: ```ruby
405: class Person < ApplicationRecord
406:   validates :email, confirmation: true
407:   validates :email_confirmation, presence: true, if: :email_changed?
408: end
409: ```
410: 
411: ### `comparison`
412: 
413: This check will validate a comparison between any two comparable values.
414: 
415: ```ruby
416: class Promotion < ApplicationRecord
417:   validates :end_date, comparison: { greater_than: :start_date }
418: end
419: ```
420: 
421: The default error message for this helper is _"failed comparison"_.
422: You can also pass in a custom message via the `message` option.
423: 
424: These options are all supported:
425: 
426: * `:greater_than` - Specifies the value must be greater than the supplied
427:   value. The default error message for this option is _"must be greater than
428:   %{count}"_.
429: * `:greater_than_or_equal_to` - Specifies the value must be greater than or
430:   equal to the supplied value. The default error message for this option is
431:   _"must be greater than or equal to %{count}"_.
432: * `:equal_to` - Specifies the value must be equal to the supplied value. The
433:   default error message for this option is _"must be equal to %{count}"_.
434: * `:less_than` - Specifies the value must be less than the supplied value. The
435:   default error message for this option is _"must be less than %{count}"_.
436: * `:less_than_or_equal_to` - Specifies the value must be less than or equal to
437:   the supplied value. The default error message for this option is _"must be
438:   less than or equal to %{count}"_.
439: * `:other_than` - Specifies the value must be other than the supplied value.
440:   The default error message for this option is _"must be other than %{count}"_.
441: 
442: NOTE: The validator requires a compare option be supplied. Each option accepts a
443: value, proc, or symbol. Any class that includes Comparable can be compared.
444: 
445: ### `format`
446: 
447: This helper validates the attributes' values by testing whether they match a
448: given regular expression, which is specified using the `:with` option.
449: 
450: ```ruby
451: class Product < ApplicationRecord
452:   validates :legacy_code, format: { with: /\A[a-zA-Z]+\z/,
453:     message: "only allows letters" }
454: end
455: ```
456: 
457: Inversely, by using the `:without` option instead you can require that the
458: specified attribute does _not_ match the regular expression.
459: 
460: In either case, the provided `:with` or `:without` option must be a regular
461: expression or a proc or lambda that return one.
462: 
463: The default error message is _"is invalid"_.
464: 
465: WARNING. use `\A` and `\z` to match the start and end of the string, `^` and `$`
466: match the start/end of a line. Due to frequent misuse of `^` and `$`, you need
467: to pass the `multiline: true` option in case you use any of these two anchors in
468: the provided regular expression. In most cases, you should be using `\A` and
469: `\z`.
470: 
471: ### `inclusion`
472: 
473: This helper validates that the attributes' values are included in a given set.
474: In fact, this set can be any enumerable object.
475: 
476: ```ruby
477: class Coffee < ApplicationRecord
478:   validates :size, inclusion: { in: %w(small medium large),
479:     message: "%{value} is not a valid size" }
480: end
481: ```
482: 
483: The `inclusion` helper has an option `:in` that receives the set of values that
484: will be accepted. The `:in` option has an alias called `:within` that you can
485: use for the same purpose, if you'd like to. The previous example uses the
486: `:message` option to show how you can include the attribute's value. For full
487: options please see the [message documentation](#message).
488: 
489: The default error message for this helper is _"is not included in the list"_.
490: 
491: ### `exclusion`
492: 
493: The opposite of `inclusion` is... `exclusion`!
494: 
495: This helper validates that the attributes' values are not included in a given
496: set. In fact, this set can be any enumerable object.
497: 
498: ```ruby
499: class Account < ApplicationRecord
500:   validates :subdomain, exclusion: { in: %w(www us ca jp),
501:     message: "%{value} is reserved." }
502: end
503: ```
504: 
505: The `exclusion` helper has an option `:in` that receives the set of values that
506: will not be accepted for the validated attributes. The `:in` option has an
507: alias called `:within` that you can use for the same purpose, if you'd like to.
508: This example uses the `:message` option to show how you can include the
509: attribute's value. For full options to the message argument please see the
510: [message documentation](#message).
511: 
512: The default error message is _"is reserved"_.
513: 
514: Alternatively to a traditional enumerable (like an Array), you can supply a
515: proc, lambda, or symbol which returns an enumerable. If the enumerable is a
516: numerical, time, or datetime range the test is performed with `Range#cover?`,
517: otherwise with `include?`. When using a proc or lambda the instance under
518: validation is passed as an argument.
519: 
520: ### `length`
521: 
522: This helper validates the length of the attributes' values. It provides a
523: variety of options, so you can specify length constraints in different ways:
524: 
525: ```ruby
526: class Person < ApplicationRecord
527:   validates :name, length: { minimum: 2 }
528:   validates :bio, length: { maximum: 500 }
529:   validates :password, length: { in: 6..20 }
530:   validates :registration_number, length: { is: 6 }
531: end
532: ```
533: 
534: The possible length constraint options are:
535: 
536: * `:minimum` - The attribute cannot have less than the specified length.
537: * `:maximum` - The attribute cannot have more than the specified length.
538: * `:in` (or `:within`) - The attribute length must be included in a given
539:   interval. The value for this option must be a range.
540: * `:is` - The attribute length must be equal to the given value.
541: 
542: The default error messages depend on the type of length validation being
543: performed. You can customize these messages using the `:wrong_length`,
544: `:too_long`, and `:too_short` options and `%{count}` as a placeholder for the
545: number corresponding to the length constraint being used. You can still use the
546: `:message` option to specify an error message.
547: 
548: ```ruby
549: class Person < ApplicationRecord
550:   validates :bio, length: { maximum: 1000,
551:     too_long: "%{count} characters is the maximum allowed" }
552: end
553: ```
554: 
555: Note that the default error messages are plural (e.g., "is too short (minimum
556: is %{count} characters)"). For this reason, when `:minimum` is 1 you should
557: provide a custom message or use `presence: true` instead. When
558: `:in` or `:within` have a lower limit of 1, you should either provide a
559: custom message or call `presence` prior to `length`.
560: 
561: NOTE: Only one constraint option can be used at a time apart from the `:minimum`
562: and `:maximum` options which can be combined together.
563: 
564: ### `numericality`
565: 
566: This helper validates that your attributes have only numeric values. By
567: default, it will match an optional sign followed by an integer or floating
568: point number.
569: 
570: To specify that only integer numbers are allowed, set `:only_integer` to true.
571: Then it will use the following regular expression to validate the attribute's
572: value.
573: 
574: ```ruby
575: /\A[+-]?\d+\z/
576: ```
577: 
578: Otherwise, it will try to convert the value to a number using `Float`. `Float`s
579: are cast to `BigDecimal` using the column's precision value or a maximum of 15
580: digits.
581: 
582: ```ruby
583: class Player < ApplicationRecord
584:   validates :points, numericality: true
585:   validates :games_played, numericality: { only_integer: true }
586: end
587: ```
588: 
589: The default error message for `:only_integer` is _"must be an integer"_.
590: 
591: Besides `:only_integer`, this helper also accepts the `:only_numeric` option
592: which specifies the value must be an instance of `Numeric` and attempts to parse
593: the value if it is a `String`.
594: 
595: NOTE: By default, `numericality` doesn't allow `nil` values. You can use
596: `allow_nil: true` option to permit it. Notice that for `Integer` and `Float`
597: columns empty strings are converted to `nil`.
598: 
599: The default error message when no options are specified is _"is not a number"_.
600: 
601: There are also many options that can be used to add constraints to acceptable
602: values:
603: 
604: * `:greater_than` - Specifies the value must be greater than the supplied
605:   value. The default error message for this option is _"must be greater than
606:   %{count}"_.
607: * `:greater_than_or_equal_to` - Specifies the value must be greater than or
608:   equal to the supplied value. The default error message for this option is
609:   _"must be greater than or equal to %{count}"_.
610: * `:equal_to` - Specifies the value must be equal to the supplied value. The
611:   default error message for this option is _"must be equal to %{count}"_.
612: * `:less_than` - Specifies the value must be less than the supplied value. The
613:   default error message for this option is _"must be less than %{count}"_.
614: * `:less_than_or_equal_to` - Specifies the value must be less than or equal to
615:   the supplied value. The default error message for this option is _"must be
616:   less than or equal to %{count}"_.
617: * `:other_than` - Specifies the value must be other than the supplied value.
618:   The default error message for this option is _"must be other than %{count}"_.
619: * `:in` - Specifies the value must be in the supplied range.
620:   The default error message for this option is _"must be in %{count}"_.
621: * `:odd` - Specifies the value must be an odd number. The default error message
622:   for this option is _"must be odd"_.
623: * `:even` - Specifies the value must be an even number. The default error
624:   message for this option is _"must be even"_.
625: 
626: ### `presence`
627: 
628: This helper validates that the specified attributes are not empty. It uses the
629: [`Object#blank?`][] method to check if the value is either `nil` or a blank
630: string, that is, a string that is either empty or consists of whitespace.
631: 
632: ```ruby
633: class Person < ApplicationRecord
634:   validates :name, :login, :email, presence: true
635: end
636: ```
637: 
638: If you want to be sure that an association is present, you'll need to test
639: whether the associated object itself is present, and not the foreign key used
640: to map the association. This way, it is not only checked that the foreign key
641: is not empty but also that the referenced object exists.
642: 
643: ```ruby
644: class Supplier < ApplicationRecord
645:   has_one :account
646:   validates :account, presence: true
647: end
648: ```
649: 
650: In order to validate associated records whose presence is required, you must
651: specify the `:inverse_of` option for the association:
652: 
653: ```ruby
654: class Order < ApplicationRecord
655:   has_many :line_items, inverse_of: :order
656: end
657: ```
658: 
659: NOTE: If you want to ensure that the association is both present and valid,
660: you also need to use `validates_associated`. More on that
661: [below](#validates-associated)
662: 
663: If you validate the presence of an object associated via a `has_one` or
664: `has_many` relationship, it will check that the object is neither `blank?` nor
665: `marked_for_destruction?`.
666: 
667: Since `false.blank?` is true, if you want to validate the presence of a boolean
668: field you should use one of the following validations:
669: 
670: ```ruby
671: # Value _must_ be true or false
672: validates :boolean_field_name, inclusion: [true, false]
673: # Value _must not_ be nil, aka true or false
674: validates :boolean_field_name, exclusion: [nil]
675: ```
676: 
677: By using one of these validations, you will ensure the value will NOT be `nil`
678: which would result in a `NULL` value in most cases.
679: 
680: The default error message is _"can't be blank"_.
681: 
682: [`Object#blank?`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Object.html#method-i-blank-3F
683: 
684: ### `absence`
685: 
686: This helper validates that the specified attributes are absent. It uses the
687: [`Object#present?`][] method to check if the value is not either nil or a blank
688: string, that is, a string that is either empty or consists of whitespace.
689: 
690: ```ruby
691: class Person < ApplicationRecord
692:   validates :name, :login, :email, absence: true
693: end
694: ```
695: 
696: If you want to be sure that an association is absent, you'll need to test
697: whether the associated object itself is absent, and not the foreign key used
698: to map the association.
699: 
700: ```ruby
701: class LineItem < ApplicationRecord
702:   belongs_to :order
703:   validates :order, absence: true
704: end
705: ```
706: 
707: In order to validate associated records whose absence is required, you must
708: specify the `:inverse_of` option for the association:
709: 
710: ```ruby
711: class Order < ApplicationRecord
712:   has_many :line_items, inverse_of: :order
713: end
714: ```
715: 
716: NOTE: If you want to ensure that the association is both present and valid,
717: you also need to use `validates_associated`. More on that
718: [below](#validates-associated)
719: 
720: If you validate the absence of an object associated via a `has_one` or
721: `has_many` relationship, it will check that the object is neither `present?` nor
722: `marked_for_destruction?`.
723: 
724: Since `false.present?` is false, if you want to validate the absence of a boolean
725: field you should use `validates :field_name, exclusion: { in: [true, false] }`.
726: 
727: The default error message is _"must be blank"_.
728: 
729: [`Object#present?`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Object.html#method-i-present-3F
730: 
731: ### `uniqueness`
732: 
733: This helper validates that the attribute's value is unique right before the
734: object gets saved.
735: 
736: ```ruby
737: class Account < ApplicationRecord
738:   validates :email, uniqueness: true
739: end
740: ```
741: 
742: The validation happens by performing an SQL query into the model's table,
743: searching for an existing record with the same value in that attribute.
744: 
745: There is a `:scope` option that you can use to specify one or more attributes that
746: are used to limit the uniqueness check:
747: 
748: ```ruby
749: class Holiday < ApplicationRecord
750:   validates :name, uniqueness: { scope: :year,
751:     message: "should happen once per year" }
752: end
753: ```
754: 
755: WARNING. This validation does not create a uniqueness constraint in the
756: database, so it may happen that two different database connections create two
757: records with the same value for a column that you intend to be unique. To avoid
758: that, you must create a unique index on that column in your database.
759: 
760: In order to add a uniqueness database constraint on your database, use the
761: [`add_index`][] statement in a migration and include the `unique: true` option.
762: 
763: Should you wish to create a database constraint to prevent possible violations
764: of a uniqueness validation using the `:scope` option, you must create a unique
765: index on both columns in your database. See [the MySQL manual][] and [the MariaDB
766: manual][] for more details about multiple column indexes, or [the PostgreSQL
767: manual][] for examples of unique constraints that refer to a group of columns.
768: 
769: There is also a `:case_sensitive` option that you can use to define whether the
770: uniqueness constraint will be case sensitive, case insensitive, or if it should
771: respect the default database collation. This option defaults to respecting the
772: default database collation.
773: 
774: ```ruby
775: class Person < ApplicationRecord
776:   validates :name, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }
777: end
778: ```
779: 
780: WARNING. Note that some databases are configured to perform case-insensitive
781: searches anyway.
782: 
783: There is a `:conditions` option that you can specify additional conditions as a
784: `WHERE` SQL fragment to limit the uniqueness constraint lookup (e.g.
785: `conditions: -> { where(status: 'active') }`).
786: 
787: The default error message is _"has already been taken"_.
788: 
789: See [`validates_uniqueness_of`][] for more information.
790: 
791: [`validates_uniqueness_of`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/Validations/ClassMethods.html#method-i-validates_uniqueness_of
792: [`add_index`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/ConnectionAdapters/SchemaStatements.html#method-i-add_index
793: [the MySQL manual]: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/en/multiple-column-indexes.html
794: [the MariaDB manual]: https://mariadb.com/kb/en/compound-composite-indexes/
795: [the PostgreSQL manual]: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/ddl-constraints.html
796: 
797: ### `validates_associated`
798: 
799: You should use this helper when your model has associations that always need to
800: be validated. Every time you try to save your object, `valid?` will be called
801: on each one of the associated objects.
802: 
803: ```ruby
804: class Library < ApplicationRecord
805:   has_many :books
806:   validates_associated :books
807: end
808: ```
809: 
810: This validation will work with all of the association types.
811: 
812: CAUTION: Don't use `validates_associated` on both ends of your associations.
813: They would call each other in an infinite loop.
814: 
815: The default error message for [`validates_associated`][] is _"is invalid"_. Note
816: that each associated object will contain its own `errors` collection; errors do
817: not bubble up to the calling model.
818: 
819: NOTE: [`validates_associated`][] can only be used with ActiveRecord objects,
820: everything up until now can also be used on any object which includes
821: [`ActiveModel::Validations`][].
822: 
823: [`validates_associated`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/Validations/ClassMethods.html#method-i-validates_associated
824: 
825: ### `validates_each`
826: 
827: This helper validates attributes against a block. It doesn't have a predefined
828: validation function. You should create one using a block, and every attribute
829: passed to [`validates_each`][] will be tested against it.
830: 
831: In the following example, we will reject names and surnames that begin with
832: lower case.
833: 
834: ```ruby
835: class Person < ApplicationRecord
836:   validates_each :name, :surname do |record, attr, value|
837:     record.errors.add(attr, 'must start with upper case') if /\A[[:lower:]]/.match?(value)
838:   end
839: end
840: ```
841: 
842: The block receives the record, the attribute's name, and the attribute's value.
843: 
844: You can do anything you like to check for valid data within the block. If your
845: validation fails, you should add an error to the model, therefore making it
846: invalid.
847: 
848: [`validates_each`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validations/ClassMethods.html#method-i-validates_each
849: 
850: ### `validates_with`
851: 
852: This helper passes the record to a separate class for validation.
853: 
854: ```ruby
855: class GoodnessValidator < ActiveModel::Validator
856:   def validate(record)
857:     if record.first_name == "Evil"
858:       record.errors.add :base, "This person is evil"
859:     end
860:   end
861: end
862: 
863: class Person < ApplicationRecord
864:   validates_with GoodnessValidator
865: end
866: ```
867: 
868: There is no default error message for `validates_with`. You must manually add
869: errors to the record's errors collection in the validator class.
870: 
871: NOTE: Errors added to `record.errors[:base]` relate to the state of the record
872: as a whole.
873: 
874: To implement the validate method, you must accept a `record` parameter in the
875: method definition, which is the record to be validated.
876: 
877: If you want to add an error on a specific attribute, pass it as the first
878: argument, such as `record.errors.add(:first_name, "please choose another
879: name")`. We will cover [validation errors](#working-with-validation-errors) in greater detail later.
880: 
881: ```ruby
882: def validate(record)
883:   if record.some_field != "acceptable"
884:     record.errors.add :some_field, "this field is unacceptable"
885:   end
886: end
887: ```
888: 
889: The [`validates_with`][] helper takes a class, or a list of classes to use for
890: validation.
891: 
892: ```ruby
893: class Person < ApplicationRecord
894:   validates_with MyValidator, MyOtherValidator, on: :create
895: end
896: ```
897: 
898: Like all other validations, `validates_with` takes the `:if`, `:unless` and
899: `:on` options. If you pass any other options, it will send those options to the
900: validator class as `options`:
901: 
902: ```ruby
903: class GoodnessValidator < ActiveModel::Validator
904:   def validate(record)
905:     if options[:fields].any? { |field| record.send(field) == "Evil" }
906:       record.errors.add :base, "This person is evil"
907:     end
908:   end
909: end
910: 
911: class Person < ApplicationRecord
912:   validates_with GoodnessValidator, fields: [:first_name, :last_name]
913: end
914: ```
915: 
916: Note that the validator will be initialized *only once* for the whole application
917: life cycle, and not on each validation run, so be careful about using instance
918: variables inside it.
919: 
920: If your validator is complex enough that you want instance variables, you can
921: easily use a plain old Ruby object instead:
922: 
923: ```ruby
924: class Person < ApplicationRecord
925:   validate do |person|
926:     GoodnessValidator.new(person).validate
927:   end
928: end
929: 
930: class GoodnessValidator
931:   def initialize(person)
932:     @person = person
933:   end
934: 
935:   def validate
936:     if some_complex_condition_involving_ivars_and_private_methods?
937:       @person.errors.add :base, "This person is evil"
938:     end
939:   end
940: 
941:   # ...
942: end
943: ```
944: 
945: We will cover [custom validations](#performing-custom-validations) more later.
946: 
947: [`validates_with`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validations/ClassMethods.html#method-i-validates_with
948: 
949: Common Validation Options
950: -------------------------
951: 
952: There are several common options supported by the validators we just went over,
953: let's go over some of them now!
954: 
955: NOTE: Not all of these options are supported by every validator, please refer to
956: the API documentation for [`ActiveModel::Validations`][].
957: 
958: By using any of the validation methods we just mentioned, there also is a list
959: of common options shared along with validators. We will cover these now!
960: 
961: * [`:allow_nil`](#allow-nil): Skip validation if the attribute is `nil`.
962: * [`:allow_blank`](#allow-blank): Skip validation if the attribute is blank.
963: * [`:message`](#message): Specify a custom error message.
964: * [`:on`](#on): Specify the contexts where this validation is active.
965: * [`:strict`](#strict-validations): Raise an exception when the validation
966:   fails.
967: * [`:if` and `:unless`](#conditional-validation): Specify when the validation
968:   should or should not occur.
969: 
970: [`ActiveModel::Validations`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validations.html
971: 
972: ### `:allow_nil`
973: 
974: The `:allow_nil` option skips the validation when the value being validated is
975: `nil`.
976: 
977: ```ruby
978: class Coffee < ApplicationRecord
979:   validates :size, inclusion: { in: %w(small medium large),
980:     message: "%{value} is not a valid size" }, allow_nil: true
981: end
982: ```
983: 
984: ```irb
985: irb> Coffee.create(size: nil).valid?
986: => true
987: irb> Coffee.create(size: "mega").valid?
988: => false
989: ```
990: 
991: For full options to the message argument please see the
992: [message documentation](#message).
993: 
994: ### `:allow_blank`
995: 
996: The `:allow_blank` option is similar to the `:allow_nil` option. This option
997: will let validation pass if the attribute's value is `blank?`, like `nil` or an
998: empty string for example.
999: 
1000: ```ruby
1001: class Topic < ApplicationRecord
1002:   validates :title, length: { is: 5 }, allow_blank: true
1003: end
1004: ```
1005: 
1006: ```irb
1007: irb> Topic.create(title: "").valid?
1008: => true
1009: irb> Topic.create(title: nil).valid?
1010: => true
1011: ```
1012: 
1013: ### `:message`
1014: 
1015: As you've already seen, the `:message` option lets you specify the message that
1016: will be added to the `errors` collection when validation fails. When this
1017: option is not used, Active Record will use the respective default error message
1018: for each validation helper.
1019: 
1020: The `:message` option accepts either a `String` or `Proc` as its value.
1021: 
1022: A `String` `:message` value can optionally contain any/all of `%{value}`,
1023: `%{attribute}`, and `%{model}` which will be dynamically replaced when
1024: validation fails. This replacement is done using the i18n gem, and the
1025: placeholders must match exactly, no spaces are allowed.
1026: 
1027: ```ruby
1028: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1029:   # Hard-coded message
1030:   validates :name, presence: { message: "must be given please" }
1031: 
1032:   # Message with dynamic attribute value. %{value} will be replaced
1033:   # with the actual value of the attribute. %{attribute} and %{model}
1034:   # are also available.
1035:   validates :age, numericality: { message: "%{value} seems wrong" }
1036: end
1037: ```
1038: 
1039: A `Proc` `:message` value is given two arguments: the object being validated, and
1040: a hash with `:model`, `:attribute`, and `:value` key-value pairs.
1041: 
1042: ```ruby
1043: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1044:   validates :username,
1045:     uniqueness: {
1046:       # object = person object being validated
1047:       # data = { model: "Person", attribute: "Username", value: <username> }
1048:       message: ->(object, data) do
1049:         "Hey #{object.name}, #{data[:value]} is already taken."
1050:       end
1051:     }
1052: end
1053: ```
1054: 
1055: ### `:on`
1056: 
1057: The `:on` option lets you specify when the validation should happen. The
1058: default behavior for all the built-in validation helpers is to be run on save
1059: (both when you're creating a new record and when you're updating it). If you
1060: want to change it, you can use `on: :create` to run the validation only when a
1061: new record is created or `on: :update` to run the validation only when a record
1062: is updated.
1063: 
1064: ```ruby
1065: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1066:   # it will be possible to update email with a duplicated value
1067:   validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :create
1068: 
1069:   # it will be possible to create the record with a non-numerical age
1070:   validates :age, numericality: true, on: :update
1071: 
1072:   # the default (validates on both create and update)
1073:   validates :name, presence: true
1074: end
1075: ```
1076: 
1077: You can also use `on:` to define custom contexts. Custom contexts need to be
1078: triggered explicitly by passing the name of the context to `valid?`,
1079: `invalid?`, or `save`.
1080: 
1081: ```ruby
1082: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1083:   validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :account_setup
1084:   validates :age, numericality: true, on: :account_setup
1085: end
1086: ```
1087: 
1088: ```irb
1089: irb> person = Person.new(age: 'thirty-three')
1090: irb> person.valid?
1091: => true
1092: irb> person.valid?(:account_setup)
1093: => false
1094: irb> person.errors.messages
1095: => {:email=>["has already been taken"], :age=>["is not a number"]}
1096: ```
1097: 
1098: `person.valid?(:account_setup)` executes both the validations without saving
1099: the model. `person.save(context: :account_setup)` validates `person` in the
1100: `account_setup` context before saving.
1101: 
1102: Passing an array of symbols is also acceptable.
1103: 
1104: ```ruby
1105: class Book
1106:   include ActiveModel::Validations
1107: 
1108:   validates :title, presence: true, on: [:update, :ensure_title]
1109: end
1110: ```
1111: 
1112: ```irb
1113: irb> book = Book.new(title: nil)
1114: irb> book.valid?
1115: => true
1116: irb> book.valid?(:ensure_title)
1117: => false
1118: irb> book.errors.messages
1119: => {:title=>["can't be blank"]}
1120: ```
1121: 
1122: When triggered by an explicit context, validations are run for that context,
1123: as well as any validations _without_ a context.
1124: 
1125: ```ruby
1126: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1127:   validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :account_setup
1128:   validates :age, numericality: true, on: :account_setup
1129:   validates :name, presence: true
1130: end
1131: ```
1132: 
1133: ```irb
1134: irb> person = Person.new
1135: irb> person.valid?(:account_setup)
1136: => false
1137: irb> person.errors.messages
1138: => {:email=>["has already been taken"], :age=>["is not a number"], :name=>["can't be blank"]}
1139: ```
1140: 
1141: We will cover more use-cases for `on:` in the [callbacks guide](active_record_callbacks.html).
1142: 
1143: Strict Validations
1144: ------------------
1145: 
1146: You can also specify validations to be strict and raise
1147: `ActiveModel::StrictValidationFailed` when the object is invalid.
1148: 
1149: ```ruby
1150: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1151:   validates :name, presence: { strict: true }
1152: end
1153: ```
1154: 
1155: ```irb
1156: irb> Person.new.valid?
1157: ActiveModel::StrictValidationFailed: Name can't be blank
1158: ```
1159: 
1160: There is also the ability to pass a custom exception to the `:strict` option.
1161: 
1162: ```ruby
1163: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1164:   validates :token, presence: true, uniqueness: true, strict: TokenGenerationException
1165: end
1166: ```
1167: 
1168: ```irb
1169: irb> Person.new.valid?
1170: TokenGenerationException: Token can't be blank
1171: ```
1172: 
1173: Conditional Validation
1174: ----------------------
1175: 
1176: Sometimes it will make sense to validate an object only when a given predicate
1177: is satisfied. You can do that by using the `:if` and `:unless` options, which
1178: can take a symbol, a `Proc` or an `Array`. You may use the `:if` option when you
1179: want to specify when the validation **should** happen. Alternatively, if you
1180: want to specify when the validation **should not** happen, then you may use the
1181: `:unless` option.
1182: 
1183: ### Using a Symbol with `:if` and `:unless`
1184: 
1185: You can associate the `:if` and `:unless` options with a symbol corresponding
1186: to the name of a method that will get called right before validation happens.
1187: This is the most commonly used option.
1188: 
1189: ```ruby
1190: class Order < ApplicationRecord
1191:   validates :card_number, presence: true, if: :paid_with_card?
1192: 
1193:   def paid_with_card?
1194:     payment_type == "card"
1195:   end
1196: end
1197: ```
1198: 
1199: ### Using a Proc with `:if` and `:unless`
1200: 
1201: It is possible to associate `:if` and `:unless` with a `Proc` object
1202: which will be called. Using a `Proc` object gives you the ability to write an
1203: inline condition instead of a separate method. This option is best suited for
1204: one-liners.
1205: 
1206: ```ruby
1207: class Account < ApplicationRecord
1208:   validates :password, confirmation: true,
1209:     unless: Proc.new { |a| a.password.blank? }
1210: end
1211: ```
1212: 
1213: As `lambda` is a type of `Proc`, it can also be used to write inline conditions
1214: taking advantage of the shortened syntax.
1215: 
1216: ```ruby
1217: validates :password, confirmation: true, unless: -> { password.blank? }
1218: ```
1219: 
1220: ### Grouping Conditional Validations
1221: 
1222: Sometimes it is useful to have multiple validations use one condition. It can
1223: be easily achieved using [`with_options`][].
1224: 
1225: ```ruby
1226: class User < ApplicationRecord
1227:   with_options if: :is_admin? do |admin|
1228:     admin.validates :password, length: { minimum: 10 }
1229:     admin.validates :email, presence: true
1230:   end
1231: end
1232: ```
1233: 
1234: All validations inside of the `with_options` block will have automatically
1235: passed the condition `if: :is_admin?`
1236: 
1237: [`with_options`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Object.html#method-i-with_options
1238: 
1239: ### Combining Validation Conditions
1240: 
1241: On the other hand, when multiple conditions define whether or not a validation
1242: should happen, an `Array` can be used. Moreover, you can apply both `:if` and
1243: `:unless` to the same validation.
1244: 
1245: ```ruby
1246: class Computer < ApplicationRecord
1247:   validates :mouse, presence: true,
1248:                     if: [Proc.new { |c| c.market.retail? }, :desktop?],
1249:                     unless: Proc.new { |c| c.trackpad.present? }
1250: end
1251: ```
1252: 
1253: The validation only runs when all the `:if` conditions and none of the `:unless`
1254: conditions are evaluated to `true`.
1255: 
1256: Performing Custom Validations
1257: -----------------------------
1258: 
1259: When the built-in validation helpers are not enough for your needs, you can
1260: write your own validators or validation methods as you prefer.
1261: 
1262: ### Custom Validators
1263: 
1264: Custom validators are classes that inherit from [`ActiveModel::Validator`][].
1265: These classes must implement the `validate` method which takes a record as an
1266: argument and performs the validation on it. The custom validator is called using
1267: the `validates_with` method.
1268: 
1269: ```ruby
1270: class MyValidator < ActiveModel::Validator
1271:   def validate(record)
1272:     unless record.name.start_with? 'X'
1273:       record.errors.add :name, "Provide a name starting with X, please!"
1274:     end
1275:   end
1276: end
1277: 
1278: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1279:   validates_with MyValidator
1280: end
1281: ```
1282: 
1283: The easiest way to add custom validators for validating individual attributes
1284: is with the convenient [`ActiveModel::EachValidator`][]. In this case, the custom
1285: validator class must implement a `validate_each` method which takes three
1286: arguments: record, attribute, and value. These correspond to the instance, the
1287: attribute to be validated, and the value of the attribute in the passed
1288: instance.
1289: 
1290: ```ruby
1291: class EmailValidator < ActiveModel::EachValidator
1292:   def validate_each(record, attribute, value)
1293:     unless URI::MailTo::EMAIL_REGEXP.match?(value)
1294:       record.errors.add attribute, (options[:message] || "is not an email")
1295:     end
1296:   end
1297: end
1298: 
1299: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1300:   validates :email, presence: true, email: true
1301: end
1302: ```
1303: 
1304: As shown in the example, you can also combine standard validations with your
1305: own custom validators.
1306: 
1307: [`ActiveModel::EachValidator`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/EachValidator.html
1308: [`ActiveModel::Validator`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validator.html
1309: 
1310: ### Custom Methods
1311: 
1312: You can also create methods that verify the state of your models and add errors
1313: to the `errors` collection when they are invalid. You must then register these
1314: methods by using the [`validate`][] class method, passing in the symbols for the
1315: validation methods' names.
1316: 
1317: You can pass more than one symbol for each class method and the respective
1318: validations will be run in the same order as they were registered.
1319: 
1320: The `valid?` method will verify that the `errors` collection is empty,
1321: so your custom validation methods should add errors to it when you
1322: wish validation to fail:
1323: 
1324: ```ruby
1325: class Invoice < ApplicationRecord
1326:   validate :expiration_date_cannot_be_in_the_past,
1327:     :discount_cannot_be_greater_than_total_value
1328: 
1329:   def expiration_date_cannot_be_in_the_past
1330:     if expiration_date.present? && expiration_date < Date.today
1331:       errors.add(:expiration_date, "can't be in the past")
1332:     end
1333:   end
1334: 
1335:   def discount_cannot_be_greater_than_total_value
1336:     if discount > total_value
1337:       errors.add(:discount, "can't be greater than total value")
1338:     end
1339:   end
1340: end
1341: ```
1342: 
1343: By default, such validations will run every time you call `valid?` or save the
1344: object. But it is also possible to control when to run these custom validations
1345: by giving an `:on` option to the `validate` method, with either: `:create` or
1346: `:update`.
1347: 
1348: ```ruby
1349: class Invoice < ApplicationRecord
1350:   validate :active_customer, on: :create
1351: 
1352:   def active_customer
1353:     errors.add(:customer_id, "is not active") unless customer.active?
1354:   end
1355: end
1356: ```

1: # Rails Guides Redesign 2024
2: 
3: ## About the Project
4: 
5: The Rails Guides Visual Refresh occurred in Q1 2024, and was intended to bring the visual style of the guides inline with the rubyonrails.org site.
6: 
7: ## Editing Dependencies
8: 
9: The editing files for the Guides rebuild reside in `stylesrc` and use SCSS to improve developer experience. The code base relies on `include_media` (https://eduardoboucas.github.io/include-media/) to enable inline media-queries adjustments. We've also relied on the standard `normalize.css` (https://necolas.github.io/normalize.css/) to help bring all browsers together.
10: 
11: ## Building the Guides in Development
12: 
13: To generate new guides into static files, type `rake guides:generate` from inside the `guides` folder. If you make changes to the HTML or ERB, you'll need to remove the "output" directory before running this command. The master SCSS files (style.scss, highlight.scss) will compile as part of this process.
14: 
15: ## FAQ
16: 
17: ### Why are you not using CSS variables?
18: 
19: Per the MDN documentation on CSS custom properties (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Using_CSS_custom_properties), they are not supported in media or container queries at this point (Feb 2024). They may in future releases, and we should pivot to that when they are more wholistically supported. SCSS variables, because they are interpolated at build, serve a similar purpose and allow us the flexibility to support much older browsers.
20: 
21: ### Why do we include LTR and RTL?
22: 
23: LTR/RTL (Left to right/right to left) is a layout change based on the nature of the language the site is being displayed in. Arabic and Farsi are two well known "RTL" languages. If the site is automatically translated, then the layout will adjust (mirror horizontally) to be more in line with the text.
24: 
25: ### Why is Dark Mode in a separate file
26: 
27: IncludeMedia does not handle `prefers-color-scheme` at this time, so it was extracted.

require "active_model/validations/resolve_value"
require "active_support/core_ext/range"

module ActiveModel
  module Validations
    module Clusivity # :nodoc:
      include ResolveValue

      ERROR_MESSAGE = "An object with the method #include? or a proc, lambda or symbol is required, " \
                      "and must be supplied as the :in (or :within) option of the configuration hash"

      def check_validity!
        unless delimiter.respond_to?(:include?) || delimiter.respond_to?(:call) || delimiter.respond_to?(:to_sym)
          raise ArgumentError, ERROR_MESSAGE
        end
      end

    private
      def include?(record, value)
        members = resolve_value(record, delimiter)

        if value.is_a?(Array)
          value.all? { |v| members.public_send(inclusion_method(members), v) }
        else
          members.public_send(inclusion_method(members), value)
        end
      end

      def delimiter
        @delimiter ||= options[:in] || options[:within]
      end

      # After Ruby 2.2, <tt>Range#include?</tt> on non-number-or-time-ish ranges checks all
      # possible values in the range for equality, which is slower but more accurate.
      # <tt>Range#cover?</tt> uses the previous logic of comparing a value with the range
      # endpoints, which is fast but is only accurate on Numeric, Time, Date,
      # or DateTime ranges.
      def inclusion_method(enumerable)
        if enumerable.is_a? Range
          case enumerable.begin || enumerable.end
          when Numeric, Time, DateTime, Date
            :cover?
          else
            :include?
          end
        else
          :include?
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

Rails Internationalization (I18n) API
=====================================

The Ruby I18n (shorthand for _internationalization_) gem which is shipped with Ruby on Rails (starting from Rails 2.2) provides an easy-to-use and extensible framework for **translating your application to a single custom language** other than English or for **providing multi-language support** in your application.

The process of "internationalization" usually means to abstract all strings and other locale specific bits (such as date or currency formats) out of your application. The process of "localization" means to provide translations and localized formats for these bits.[^1]

So, in the process of _internationalizing_ your Rails application you have to:

* Ensure you have support for I18n.
* Tell Rails where to find locale dictionaries.
* Tell Rails how to set, preserve, and switch locales.

In the process of _localizing_ your application you'll probably want to do the following three things:

* Replace or supplement Rails' default locale - e.g. date and time formats, month names, Active Record model names, etc.
* Abstract strings in your application into keyed dictionaries - e.g. flash messages, static text in your views, etc.
* Store the resulting dictionaries somewhere.

This guide will walk you through the I18n API and contains a tutorial on how to internationalize a Rails application from the start.

After reading this guide, you will know:

* How I18n works in Ruby on Rails
* How to correctly use I18n in a RESTful application in various ways
* How to use I18n to translate Active Record errors or Action Mailer E-mail subjects
* Some other tools to go further with the translation process of your application

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

NOTE: The Ruby I18n framework provides you with all necessary means for internationalization/localization of your Rails application. You may also use various gems available to add additional functionality or features. See the [rails-i18n gem](https://github.com/svenfuchs/rails-i18n) for more information.

How I18n in Ruby on Rails Works
-------------------------------

Internationalization is a complex problem. Natural languages differ in so many ways (e.g. in pluralization rules) that it is hard to provide tools for solving all problems at once. For that reason the Rails I18n API focuses on:

* providing support for English and similar languages out of the box

```
### `:on`

The `:on` option lets you specify when the validation should happen. ...

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  # it will be possible to update email with a duplicated value
  validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :create
  ...
end
```

You can also use `on:` to define custom contexts. Custom contexts need to be
triggered explicitly by passing the name of the context to `valid?`,
`invalid?`, or `save`.

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :account_setup
  validates :age, numericality: true, on: :account_setup
end
```

```irb
irb> person = Person.new(age: 'thirty-three')
irb> person.valid?
=> true
irb> person.valid?(:account_setup)
=> false
irb> person.errors.messages
=> {:email=>["has already been taken"], :age=>["is not a number"]}
```

`person.valid?(:account_setup)` executes both the validations without saving
the model. `person.save(context: :account_setup)` validates `person` in the
`account_setup` context before saving.

Passing an array of symbols is also acceptable.

```ruby
class Book
  include ActiveModel::Validations

  validates :title, presence: true, on: [:update, :ensure_title]
end
```

```irb
irb> book = Book.new(title: nil)
irb> book.valid?
=> true
irb> book.valid?(:ensure_title)
=> false
irb> book.errors.messages
=> {:title=>["can't be blank"]}
```

When triggered by an explicit context, validations are run for that context,
as well as any validations _without_ a context.

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :account_setup
  validates :age, numericality: true, on: :account_setup
  validates :name, presence: true
end
```

```irb
irb> person = Person.new
irb> person.valid?(:account_setup)
=> false
irb> person.errors.messages
=> {:email=>["has already been taken"], :age=>["is not a number"], :name=>["can't be blank"]}
```

  # it will be possible to create the record with a non-numerical age
  validates :age, numericality: true, on: :update

  # the default (validates on both create and update)
  validates :name, presence: true
end
```

You can also use `on:` to define custom contexts. See [Custom
Contexts](#custom-contexts) below for more details.

### Custom Contexts

Custom contexts need to be triggered explicitly by passing the name of the
context to `valid?`, `invalid?`, or `save`.

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :account_setup
  validates :age, numericality: true, on: :account_setup
end
```

```irb
irb> person = Person.new(age: 'thirty-three')
irb> person.valid?
=> true
irb> person.valid?(:account_setup)
=> false
irb> person.errors.messages
=> {:email=>["has already been taken"], :age=>["is not a number"]}
```

`person.valid?(:account_setup)` executes both the validations without saving
the model. `person.save(context: :account_setup)` validates `person` in the
`account_setup` context before saving.

Passing an array of symbols is also acceptable.

```ruby
class Book
  include ActiveModel::Validations

  validates :title, presence: true, on: [:update, :ensure_title]
end
```

```irb
irb> book = Book.new(title: nil)
irb> book.valid?
=> true
irb> book.valid?(:ensure_title)
=> false
irb> book.errors.messages
=> {:title=>["can't be blank"]}
```

When triggered by an explicit context, validations are run for that context,
as well as any validations _without_ a context.

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :account_setup
  validates :age, numericality: true, on: :account_setup
  validates :name, presence: true
end
```

```irb
irb> person = Person.new
irb> person.valid?(:account_setup)
=> false
irb> person.errors.messages
=> {:email=>["has already been taken"], :age=>["is not a number"], :name=>["can't be blank"]}
```

### `errors.where` and Error Object

Sometimes we may need more information about each error besides its message.
Each error is encapsulated as an `ActiveModel::Error` object, and the
[`where`][] method is the most common way of access.

`where` returns an array of error objects filtered by various degrees of
conditions.

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  validates :name, presence: true, length: { minimum: 3 }
end
```

We can filter for just the `attribute` by passing it as the first parameter to
`errors.where(:attr)`. The second parameter is used for filtering the `type` of
error we want by calling `errors.where(:attr, :type)`.

```irb
irb> person = Person.new
irb> person.valid?
=> false

irb> person.errors.where(:name)
=> [ ... ] # all errors for :name attribute

irb> person.errors.where(:name, :too_short)
=> [ ... ] # :too_short errors for :name attribute
```

Lastly, we can filter by any `options` that may exist on the given type of error
object.

```irb
irb> person = Person.new
irb> person.valid?
=> false

irb> person.errors.where(:name, :too_short, minimum: 3)
=> [ ... ] # all name errors being too short and minimum is 2
```

You can read various information from these error objects:

```irb
irb> error = person.errors.where(:name).last

irb> error.attribute
=> :name
irb> error.type
=> :too_short
irb> error.options[:count]
=> 3
```

You can also generate the error message:

```irb
irb> error.message
=> "is too short (minimum is 3 characters)"
irb> error.full_message
=> "Name is too short (minimum is 3 characters)"
```

The [`full_message`][] method generates a more user-friendly message, with the
capitalized attribute name prepended. (To customize the format that
`full_message` uses, see the [I18n guide](i18n.html#active-model-methods).)

[`full_message`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Errors.html#method-i-full_message
[`where`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Errors.html#method-i-where

### `errors.add`

The [`add`][] method creates the error object by taking the `attribute`, the
error `type` and additional options hash. This is useful when writing your own
validator, as it lets you define very specific error situations.

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  validate do |person|
    errors.add :name, :too_plain, message: "is not cool enough"
  end
end
```

```irb
irb> person = Person.create
irb> person.errors.where(:name).first.type
=> :too_plain
irb> person.errors.where(:name).first.full_message
=> "Name is not cool enough"
```

[`add`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Errors.html#method-i-add
```

971: Common Validation Options
972: -------------------------
973: 
974: There are several common options supported by the validators we just went over,

976: 
977: NOTE: Not all of these options are supported by every validator, please refer to

980: By using any of the validation methods we just mentioned, there also is a list

982: 
983: * [`:allow_nil`](#allow-nil): Skip validation if the attribute is `nil`.
984: * [`:allow_blank`](#allow-blank): Skip validation if the attribute is blank.
985: * [`:message`](#message): Specify a custom error message.
986: * [`:on`](#on): Specify the contexts where this validation is active.
987: * [`:strict`](#strict-validations): Raise an exception when the validation

992: [`ActiveModel::Validations`]: https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveModel/Validations.html

994: ### `:allow_nil`
995: 
996: The `:allow_nil` option skips the validation when the value being validated is
997: `nil`.
998: 
999: ```ruby
1000: class Coffee < ApplicationRecord
1001:   validates :size, inclusion: { in: %w(small medium large),
1002:     message: "%{value} is not a valid size" }, allow_nil: true
1003: end
1004: ```
1005: 
1006: ```irb
1007: irb> Coffee.create(size: nil).valid?
1008: => true
1009: irb> Coffee.create(size: "mega").valid?
1010: => false
1011: ```
1012: 
1013: For full options to the message argument please see the
1014: [message documentation](#message).
1015: 
1016: ### `:allow_blank`
1017: 
1018: The `:allow_blank` option is similar to the `:allow_nil` option. This option
1019: will let validation pass if the attribute's value is `blank?`, like `nil` or an
1020: empty string for example.
1021: 
1022: ```ruby
1023: class Topic < ApplicationRecord
1024:   validates :title, length: { is: 5 }, allow_blank: true
1025: end
1026: ```
1027: 
1028: ```irb
1029: irb> Topic.create(title: "").valid?
1030: => true
1031: irb> Topic.create(title: nil).valid?
1032: => true
1033: ```
1034: 
1035: ### `:message`
1036: 
1037: As you've already seen, the `:message` option lets you specify the message that
1038: will be added to the `errors` collection when validation fails. When this
1039: option is not used, Active Record will use the respective default error message
1040: for each validation helper.
1041: 
1042: The `:message` option accepts either a `String` or `Proc` as its value.
1043: 
1044: A `String` `:message` value can optionally contain any/all of `%{value}`,
1045: `%{attribute}`, and `%{model}` which will be dynamically replaced when
1046: validation fails. This replacement is done using the i18n gem, and the
1047: placeholders must match exactly, no spaces are allowed.
1048: 
1049: ```ruby
1050: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1051:   # Hard-coded message
1052:   validates :name, presence: { message: "must be given please" }
1053: 
1054:   # Message with dynamic attribute value. %{value} will be replaced
1055:   # with the actual value of the attribute. %{attribute} and %{model}
1056:   # are also available.
1057:   validates :age, numericality: { message: "%{value} seems wrong" }
1058: end
1059: ```
1060: 
1061: A `Proc` `:message` value is given two arguments: the object being validated, and
1062: a hash with `:model`, `:attribute`, and `:value` key-value pairs.
1063: 
1064: ```ruby
1065: class Person < ApplicationRecord
1066:   validates :username,
1067:     uniqueness: {
1068:       # object = person object being validated
1069:       # data = { model: "Person", attribute: "Username", value: <username> }
1070:       message: ->(object, data) do
1071:         "Hey #{object.name}, #{data[:value]} is already taken."
1072:       end
1073:     }
1074: end
1075: ```

1077: ### `:on`
1078: 
1079: The `:on` option lets you specify when the validation should happen. The

You can also use `on:` to define custom contexts. Custom contexts need to be
triggered explicitly by passing the name of the context to `valid?`,
`invalid?`, or `save`. See [Custom Contexts](#custom-contexts) below for more
details.

### Custom Contexts

Custom contexts allow you to group validations and run them in a specific
situation. They are triggered explicitly by passing the context name to
`valid?`, `invalid?`, or `save`.

```ruby
class Person < ApplicationRecord
  validates :email, uniqueness: true, on: :account_setup
  validates :age, numericality: true, on: :account_setup
end
```

```irb
irb> person = Person.new(age: 'thirty-three')
irb> person.valid?
=> true
irb> person.valid?(:account_setup)
=> false
irb> person.errors.messages
=> {:email=>["has already been taken"], :age=>["is not a number"]}
```

`person.valid?(:account_setup)` executes both the validations without saving
the model. `person.save(context: :account_setup)` validates `person` in the
`account_setup` context before saving.

Passing an array of symbols is also acceptable.

```ruby
class Book
  include ActiveModel::Validations

  validates :title, presence: true, on: [:update, :ensure_title]
end
```

```irb
irb> book = Book.new(title: nil)
irb> book.valid?
=> true
irb> book.valid?(:ensure_title)
=> false
irb> book.errors.messages
=> {:title=>["can't be blank"]}
```

When triggered by an explicit context, validations are run for that context,
as well as any validations _without_ a context.

44: ### Why Use Validations?
45: 
46: Validations are used to ensure that only valid data is saved into your

48: every user provides a valid email address and mailing address. Model-level
49: validations are the best way to ensure that only valid data is saved into your

51: convenient to test and maintain. Rails provides built-in helpers for common
52: needs, and allows you to create your own validation methods as well.

54: ### Alternate Ways to Validate

56: There are several other ways to validate data before it is saved into your
57: database, including native database constraints, client-side validations and
58: controller-level validations. Here's a summary of the pros and cons:
59: 
60: * Database constraints and/or stored procedures make the validation mechanisms
61:   database-dependent and can make testing and maintenance more difficult.
62:   However, if your database is used by other applications, it may be a good
63:   idea to use some constraints at the database level. Additionally,
64:   database-level validations can safely handle some things (such as uniqueness
65:   in heavily-used tables) that can be difficult to implement otherwise.
66: * Client-side validations can be useful, but are generally unreliable if used
67:   alone. If they are implemented using JavaScript, they may be bypassed if
68:   JavaScript is turned off in the user's browser. However, if combined with
69:   other techniques, client-side validation can be a convenient way to provide
70:   users with immediate feedback as they use your site.
71: * Controller-level validations can be tempting to use, but often become
72:   unwieldy and difficult to test and maintain. Whenever possible, it's a good
73:   idea to keep your controllers simple, as it will make your
74:   application a pleasure to work with in the long run.

77: that model-level validations are the most appropriate in most circumstances.

34:

Retrieving Objects from the Database
------------------------------------

To retrieve objects from the database, Active Record provides several finder methods. Each finder method allows you to pass arguments into it to perform certain queries on your database without writing raw SQL.

The methods are:

* [`annotate`][]
* [`find`][]
* [`create_with`][]
* [`distinct`][]
* [`eager_load`][]
* [`extending`][]

**DO NOT READ THIS FILE ON GITHUB, GUIDES ARE PUBLISHED ON https://guides.rubyonrails.org.**

Active Record Query Interface
=============================

This guide covers different ways to retrieve data from the database using Active Record.

After reading this guide, you will know:

* How to find records using a variety of methods and conditions.
* How to specify the order, retrieved attributes, grouping, and other properties of the found records.
* How to use eager loading to reduce the number of database queries needed for data retrieval.
* How to use dynamic finder methods.
* How to use method chaining to use multiple Active Record methods together.
* How to check for the existence of particular records.
* How to perform various calculations on Active Record models.
* How to run EXPLAIN on relations.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

What is the Active Record Query Interface?
------------------------------------------

If you're used to using raw SQL to find database records, then you will generally find that there are better ways to carry out the same operations in Rails. Active Record insulates you from the need to use SQL in most cases.

Active Record will perform queries on the database for you and is compatible with most database systems, including MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, and SQLite. Regardless of which database system you're using, the Active Record method format will always be the same.

Code examples throughout this guide will refer to one or more of the following models:

TIP: All of the following models use `id` as the primary key, unless specified otherwise.

```ruby
class Author < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :books, -> { order(year_published: :desc) }
end
```

```ruby
class Book < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :supplier
  belongs_to :author
  has_many :reviews
  has_and_belongs_to_many :orders, join_table: 'books_orders'

  scope :in_print, -> { where(out_of_print: false) }
  scope :out_of_print, -> { where(out_of_print: true) }
  scope :old, -> { where(year_published: ...50.years.ago.year) }
  scope :out_of_print_and_expensive, -> { out_of_print.where('price > 500') }
  scope :costs_more_than, ->(amount) { where('price > ?', amount) }
end
```

```ruby
class Customer < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :orders
  has_many :reviews
end
```

```ruby
class Order < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :customer
  has_and_belongs_to_many :books, join_table: 'books_orders'

  enum :status, [:shipped, :being_packed, :complete, :cancelled]

  scope :created_before, ->(time) { where(created_at: ...time) }
end
```
